title: a second drain resumes the live one instead of refusing
description:
Start a drain while another is running in the same repo and the second does not refuse. It reads run.json, finds an active run, and resumes it -- spawning a second model process per issue into the same worktrees the first one's workers are still writing.

Two writers per issue, two processes in one worktree, and both writing run.json. The first run then reported done with zero issues done.

runstate.Active's own doc names 'a second drain' as the thing it exists to stop, but drain never asked. Status cannot answer it either: a run killed mid-barrier is left active on purpose, because being resumable is the point.

Found by the concurrent-drain scenario in scripts/integrator-stress.sh.
close_reason: fixed; runstate.Hold, with a unit test and the concurrent-drain scenario

title: Unstaging the beads export once per barrier is undone by the next bd read
description:
Live drain 2, wave 4: the only issue in the wave finished, gated and reviewed, and the barrier then parked it with 'git would not merge bd-auto/kv-555.4 and left no conflicted paths: Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by merge: .beads/issues.jsonl'. beads-auto-imp-dql.9 was supposed to have fixed exactly this, and the fix is in the binary that ran.

Root cause: unstageBeadsExport() is called once, at the top of Integrate, and every bd command run after it puts the export straight back in the index. Reproduced in the lab: 'git status --porcelain -- .beads/issues.jsonl' says ' M', 'bd show <id>' is run, and it says 'M '. A read command re-exports and git-adds. candidates() calls e.BD.Show for every candidate, between the unstage and the merge, so by the time git merge runs the index is dirty again and ort refuses.

The unstage has to happen immediately before the merge itself, not once per barrier. Verified by hand in the failing lab repo: reset HEAD -- .beads, then the identical merge command succeeds.
acceptance_criteria: unstageBeadsExport runs immediately before each git merge; a regression test that stages a beads export between the top of Integrate and the merge (as a bd read does) still merges cleanly.
close_reason: unstageBeadsExport now runs immediately before every merge, not once per barrier; regression test TestBDStagingTheExportAgainMidBarrierDoesNotStopTheMerge, and the exact merge that parked kv-555.4 in the lab now reports 1 merged, 0 parked, gate passed

title: a worker's commit stages the beads export into the main checkout, and the next barrier cannot merge anything
description:
Found by the live kv-ctf drain, which finished three issues — all gated, all reviewed, all committed — and parked two of them at the wave 2 barrier with:

    git merge --no-ff --no-edit bd-auto/kv-ctf.2: exit status 2:
    error: Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by merge:
      .beads/issues.jsonl

The chain, reproduced by hand:

1. A worker commits in its own worktree. Its git is not suppressed — deliberately, because beads' pre-commit is what keeps the export in step — so beads' pre-commit hook runs.
2. bd exports .beads/issues.jsonl and stages it. The export lives in the main checkout, and so does the index it is staged into: a commit inside .beads/auto/wt/<issue> leaves  staged in the main checkout, not in the worktree that made the commit.
3. The barrier merges into the epic branch in that main checkout. git refuses to merge while a path in the index differs from HEAD, even when the branch being merged does not touch that path — ort writes a fresh index and will not overwrite a staged change.

Every branch after the first worker commit therefore fails to merge, is recorded as parked, and the handoff is refused over work that was already finished. The run reported  above a table whose three rows all said done.

Verified both halves separately: with the export merely modified in the working tree the same merge succeeds; staged, it fails. The workaround in this repo's own history is a human running  between waves — see the two commits named 'bd: export issue state ahead of <issue> merge'.
design: The staged export is a passive re-export of the Dolt database, regenerable with bd export, and it was staged by a hook that bd-auto's own worker fired. Unstaging it before the merge costs nothing and loses nothing: the working tree keeps the file exactly as it is, and nothing is committed on anyone's behalf. Scope it to paths under .beads/ so no other staged work is touched, and say what was unstaged.
acceptance_criteria: A barrier merges cleanly with the beads export staged in the main checkout; the working tree copy is left alone; only .beads paths are unstaged; a test stages an export and asserts the merge lands rather than parking.
close_reason: drain 1 re-ran green on the fixed binary: 2 waves, 3 issues, epic closed, branch pushed to the local remote and a pull request opened through the shim; 61 turns and $3.04 recorded

title: Spike: verify concurrent bd writes from N worktrees
description:
Before anything else, prove that 5 concurrent processes can safely hit the one embedded Dolt DB from 5 different git worktrees. Everything else in this epic assumes it.

Test: create 5 worktrees, run bd ready --claim simultaneously from all of them against a pool of 5 open issues, and confirm each process claims a DIFFERENT issue with no errors, no lock timeouts and no corruption. Repeat for concurrent bd close, bd note and bd create.

If direct embedded mode does not hold up, evaluate the alternatives bd already ships: the auto-started Dolt server (see the dolt-server.* entries in .beads/.gitignore), bd --global shared-server mode, and --dolt-auto-commit=batch. Record the verdict in the design field of the epic.
acceptance_criteria: 5 concurrent claims return 5 distinct issue IDs, zero errors, DB passes bd doctor afterwards. Chosen concurrency mode documented on the epic.
notes:
SPIKE RESULT: PASS, with one hard constraint discovered.

Setup: 5 git worktrees, 5 concurrent processes, embedded Dolt (mode: direct), bd 1.0.4, 16 cores.

PASS - concurrent bd ready --claim from 5 worktrees: 5 distinct issues claimed, each assigned to its own actor, all rc=0, empty stderr. The atomic claim holds under real contention. This is the pull-queue guarantee the whole design rests on.
PASS - concurrent bd note + bd close, each worker on ITS OWN issue: 10/10 rc=0, no lock errors, no timeouts.
PASS - concurrent bd create from 5 worktrees: 5 distinct IDs, no collisions.
PASS - bd resolves the main repo .beads/ from every worktree; no per-worktree setup needed.

FAIL - concurrent writes to the SAME issue silently lose data. 5 workers ran bd note against one issue; all 5 returned rc=0 but only 4 notes landed (worker 3 was lost). bd note is a read-modify-write on a text field with no locking, and the exit code does not report the loss.

VERDICT: embedded direct mode is fine at concurrency 5. No Dolt server, no --global, no --dolt-auto-commit=batch needed. bd doctor is unsupported in embedded mode, so integrity checks must use bd list/bd show instead.

RULE THIS IMPOSES ON THE DESIGN: exactly one writer per issue at any time. The architecture already gives us this (one worker owns one issue), but it must be enforced, not assumed:
- The orchestrator must never append notes to an issue while its worker is running. Retry/failure notes are written only after the worker has finished.
- The integrator writes to wave issues only after every worker in the wave has finished.
- Shared run state stays in .beads/auto/run.json, owned by the orchestrator alone. Never model shared state as a shared bead.
close_reason: Spike complete: embedded direct mode safe at concurrency 5; single-writer-per-issue rule discovered and recorded

title: a wave run with nothing to dispatch reports done without merging anything
description:
Start a wave-scheduled drain again when every issue is already closed and its branches are still unmerged -- what a barrier stopped by a dirty checkout leaves behind, or a killed run -- and drainInWaves sees an empty wave, breaks out of the loop, and reports 'run finished after 0 wave(s): 4 done, 0 parked'.

Nothing was merged. Every branch is still standing, the epic branch is untouched, and the report says the run succeeded.

drainContinuously does not have this: it settles leftovers before its first worker. The wave loop had no counterpart.

Found by the dirty-checkout recovery step in scripts/integrator-stress.sh.
close_reason: fixed; unit test plus the dirty-checkout recovery scenario

title: a run killed inside the barrier cannot be resumed
description:
Kill a drain while the integrator is resolving a conflict and it cannot be restarted, even though resuming from .beads/auto/run.json is the design's headline claim.

Two things block it:

1. The workers had already closed their issues, so bd offers no open children under the epic and 'drain' refuses with 'nothing to drain'. The scope is derived from bd, never from the run that is still marked active.
2. Past that, the barrier refuses because the checkout is mid-merge -- a merge bd-auto itself started and was killed inside. The tool that made the state is the one thing that will not clear it.

The result is branches nobody merged, a checkout stuck mid-merge, and no command that finishes it short of git surgery.

Found by the resume scenario in scripts/integrator-stress.sh.
close_reason: fixed; covered by the resume scenario and two unit tests

title: the barrier gives up when the export blocks the merge after it was cleared
description:
Two shapes of git refusal over .beads exports still stop the barrier dead.

1. Continuous scheduling integrates a lane while the other workers run, so bd can rewrite the export in the window between clearBeadsExport() and git merge. Clearing beforehand is a race the barrier can lose.
2. Until the first export is committed, HEAD does not have the path at all. The branch adds it, an untracked re-export sits where it wants to land, and git refuses with 'untracked working tree files would be overwritten' — which restoring from HEAD cannot answer.

Either way the whole wave lands nowhere: 4 done, 0 merged, run left active.

Found by scripts/integrator-stress.sh, a provider:fake drain that reproduces both end to end.
close_reason: fixed in 836114a; scripts/integrator-stress.sh covers both shapes end to end

title: integrate: git switch to epic branch fails on dirty beads export in working tree
description:
## Steps to Reproduce
1. Drain an epic with handoff.branch on (default) so an epic branch is created and reused across waves.
2. Between barrier calls, any plain bd command (even a read-only 'bd show') re-exports the Dolt DB and rewrites .beads/issues.jsonl and .beads/interactions.jsonl on disk in the main checkout's working tree.
3. Reach a wave where stage() (internal/drain/integrate.go:337) needs to 'git switch' onto the already-existing epic branch (checkout isn't currently on it).
4. git refuses: 'Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by checkout: .beads/interactions.jsonl .beads/issues.jsonl' -- the barrier errors out and the whole run fails, even though every issue in the wave already finished.

Observed live on beads-auto-imp-04l wave 3: 5/7 issues done, run failed after the git switch to bd-auto/epic/run-20260818-152457.

## Root Cause
unstageBeadsExport() (internal/drain/integrate.go:370) only removes the two beads export files from the index -- its own doc comment says the working-tree copy is deliberately left untouched, because it was built to fix git merge's ort-strategy refusal on a *staged* path. git switch is a different check: it refuses on ANY uncommitted diff from HEAD (staged or not) when the target branch's committed copy differs. The working-tree rewrite from a re-export is exactly that case, and unstageBeadsExport does nothing to fix it.
design: These two files are an explicitly disposable, regenerable export of the Dolt DB (same reasoning already used to justify unstaging them for merges). Extend unstageBeadsExport (or add a sibling step) to also discard the working-tree diff -- e.g. 'git checkout -- .beads/issues.jsonl .beads/interactions.jsonl' or 'git restore --staged --worktree -- .beads' -- immediately before stage()'s git switch calls in integrate.go. Also worth a quick look: why the main checkout was off the epic branch at wave 3 at all, given stage()'s comment says the checkout stays on the epic branch between waves.
acceptance_criteria: A regression test reproduces a dirty .beads/*.jsonl working tree (simulating a bd show re-export) immediately before stage() switches onto an already-existing epic branch, and the switch succeeds without discarding unrelated working-tree changes elsewhere in the checkout.
close_reason: Fixed on the epic branch: clear the regenerable Beads export before branch switches and merges; covered by dirty-export regression tests.

title: Under autonomy: auto, keep N workers in flight continuously instead of draining wave by wave
description:
## What is wanted

In autonomous mode the run should hold `concurrency` workers busy for as long as there is anything in scope to work on. A slot that frees gets refilled from whatever is ready right now. There is no point at which the run gathers everything, stops, and starts again — the scheduler is a steady state, not a sequence of batches.

## What is actually there today

Half of this already exists and should not be rebuilt: a wave is already a cap rather than a batch. `waveRun.topUp` (internal/drain/drain_wave.go:577) is called by every worker as it finishes, re-asks bd what is ready, and dispatches into the freed slot within the same wave. The README says so at 'A wave is not a fixed list'.

Two things still stop the world, and they are what this issue is about.

1. **The barrier is a join.** `Drain` (internal/drain/drain_wave.go:141) runs `runWave` to completion — `w.wg.Wait()` — before `barrier` merges anything. So the last long worker in a wave leaves every other slot empty until it lands, and then nothing runs at all while the integrator merges each branch and runs the wave gate on the merged result. On a scope with one slow issue per wave that is most of the wall clock.
2. **A dependent cannot join the wave it depends on.** `wave.Joinable` (internal/wave/plan.go:197) drops any ready issue that depends on an issue still in `WaveIssues`, and it is right to: the dependency's branch is not in HEAD until the barrier merges it, so the worker would implement against a tree its dependency's work is missing from. Dependents therefore wait for a barrier even when their dependency finished first and there are free slots.

## The shape of the change

Integrate per issue rather than per wave. When a worker lands, merge its branch onto the epic branch and gate the merged result, serialised behind a single integrator lock; on success it is in HEAD, so anything that depended on it becomes genuinely dispatchable and the joinable filter relaxes from 'depends on an in-flight sibling' to 'depends on something not yet merged into HEAD'. Readiness is recomputed on each completion and on each merge. Workers keep running while a merge happens — the merge is in the main checkout and workers are in their own worktrees, but this is the first time the two overlap, so the gate's load and any assumption of a quiet tree need checking.

One thing gets simpler: `blameGate`/`remergePeeled` (internal/drain/integrate.go:794, :875) exist to work out which of several merges turned the wave gate red. Merging one branch at a time makes the offender known. That machinery still has to stay for `bd-auto integrate --all`, which is the manual multi-branch path.

## What must not break

- **`autonomy: wave` keeps its barrier.** That mode exists to put a human between waves (README: 'four genuinely independent issues, with --autonomy wave'), and `pauseAtBarrier` is where it stops. Continuous scheduling is the `auto` path only, as asked.
- **`bd-auto run pause` still has somewhere to stop.** It currently 'holds the run at the next wave boundary'. With no boundary it needs a defined one — most likely: stop dispatching, let what is in flight land and integrate.
- **The outage circuit breaker.** An `OutcomeInfra` report cancels the wave (`w.cancel()`, drain_wave.go:540) so five workers do not walk into one rate limit. A run with no waves needs that as a run-level breaker, and `stopped()` must keep refusing to top up after it trips.
- **Resumability.** `.beads/auto/run.json` carries `Wave` and `WaveIssues` (internal/runstate/state.go:223) and `wave.Resume` reads them. Whatever replaces the wave number has to survive a kill and a re-run, and an existing run.json from an older binary has to still resume.
- **The runaway guard.** `DefaultMaxWaves` bounds a loop that is not progressing. Continuous scheduling needs an equivalent — a no-progress condition, not a wave count.
- **The index refresh.** `refreshIndex` runs at the barrier (integrate.go:271) precisely because the merge changed the tree. Per-issue merging needs it somewhere that does not rebuild the index N times per run for no reason; see beads-auto-imp-xhw for why it sits where it does.
- **The renderers.** `EventWaveStart`/`EventWaveEnd`/`EventWaveIntegrating` and the TUI barrier row (internal/tui/barrier.go) are all built around a wave that begins and ends. `DrainReport.Waves` and `Integrations` are in the JSON contract. A continuous run needs a shape a watcher can read — probably an integration lane alongside the workers rather than a barrier row between them.
- **One writer per issue**, and the merge/gate serialisation. Two integrations must never overlap.

## Notes

This is large enough to split; the natural seams are the scheduler, the per-issue integrator, run state and resume, and the renderers plus the report contract. Split it once the design is settled rather than now. README's 'How a run works' diagram and its wave paragraphs are part of the work, not a follow-up — they are the reference for this behaviour.
design: Serialise integration behind one lock and merge per landed issue, rather than keeping a barrier and merely overlapping the next wave's dispatch with it. The alternative — dispatch the next wave while the integrator works — leaves the same problem for dependents: they need their dependency in HEAD, and only a completed merge gives them that.
acceptance_criteria:
- Under autonomy: auto, at any moment while unblocked in-scope work remains, the number of workers in flight is the concurrency cap — including while an issue is being merged and gated.
- An issue whose only blocker was another issue in the run starts as soon as that blocker's branch is merged, without waiting for anything else in flight.
- autonomy: wave is unchanged: it still gathers, integrates and pauses for a human.
- An infra failure still stops the run from dispatching more workers.
- A killed run resumes without re-running a landed issue or double-dispatching an in-flight one.
- A run that stops making progress still terminates with a stated reason.
- make check passes; the drain tests cover a continuous run with a dependency chain and a mid-run outage, using internal/runner/fake.
notes:
bd-auto parked beads-auto-imp-04l.2 at integration: git would not merge bd-auto/beads-auto-imp-04l.2 and left no conflicted paths: git merge --no-ff --no-edit bd-auto/beads-auto-imp-04l.2: exit status 2: error: Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by merge:
	.beads/interactions.jsonl
	.beads/issues.jsonl
Please commit your changes or stash them before you merge.
Aborting
Merge with strategy ort failed.
close_reason: reviewed pass at wave 3; parked at the wave 4 barrier by beads-auto-imp-zjf, not by anything wrong with the work. Merged by hand into bd-auto/epic/run-20260818-152457 after main was merged in first, and the gate is green on the fully merged branch.

title: A question's options and the answer being typed are clipped at the terminal edge
description:
## What happened

During a live drain in another project a worker asked a question and the line ran off the right edge of the terminal. The reader could not see the whole thing, so they could not answer faithfully — they answered a question they had only partly read.

## Where it comes from

The question text itself is already wrapped (internal/tui/model.go:1085, and wrap() at :1131 carries the comment 'losing the end of it to a clip is losing the question'). What is *not* wrapped is everything around it:

- internal/tui/model.go:1096-1100 — each option line is 'N. <label> — <description>' passed through clip(), so a long label, or any label with a description behind it, loses its tail to an ellipsis. The reader then picks 1-N without having read N.
- internal/tui/model.go:1110 — the answer being typed is clip()ped from the front, so once what you have typed is wider than the box, the tail and the cursor vanish off the right edge and you are typing blind. tail() already exists at :1349 for exactly this shape of problem.
- internal/drain/bus.go:343-345 (plain renderer) — the question is collapse()d to one line and the options are joined with ' | ' behind it, on a single unwrapped line. Piped to a file this is fine; on a terminal it is one long soft-wrapped run with no structure, and it is what a --plain or non-TTY watcher gets.

## Why it matters

An unanswerable question is worse than no question: the worker is parked, the human is guessing, and the recorded answer in run.json is a guess that a resumed run will replay. Wrapping the prose but clipping the options means the reader sees the part that asks and not the part that decides.

## Also in scope

The vertical edge, if it turns out to be the same bug: questionBox() has no height cap and bodyHeight() at internal/tui/detail.go:158 only subtracts whatever height it returns, so a long question can push the option list and the key hints below the bottom of a short terminal. Worth checking against a small window before deciding whether it needs its own issue.
acceptance_criteria:
- No part of a question the reader must act on — text, option labels, option descriptions — is truncated in the TUI at any terminal width; long options wrap and indent under their number rather than being clipped.
- While typing an answer, the end of the input and the cursor stay visible however long the answer gets.
- The plain renderer emits a question in a form that stays readable on a terminal at typical widths, without breaking its one-event-one-line contract for piped output.
- A question in a short window still shows its options and the answer keys.
- Covered by tests in internal/tui (the existing ask_test.go/screenshot harness) at a narrow width and a short height.
notes:
Do not fix by shortening what a model may put in a question — the width is ours to handle, the content is not.

title: What watching a live drain showed up: an unreadable question, and idle workers at the barrier
description:

title: flob loses a run when two workers register the same schema at once, because Dolt says retry and nothing does
description:
Found by scripts/flob-stress.sh, reproduced on every run of it.

Five workers in bd-auto's worktree layout each record flob runs into the one shared store. Four of the five FIRST writes fail outright, every time. Later writes from the same workers all succeed, which is the tell: it is not load, it is one specific moment.

The traceback is the same each time:

  flob/sdk.py:511 start -> _register_schema
  flob/schema/registry.py:383 ensure_registered -> writer.append('schemas', record)
  pymysql.err.OperationalError: (1213, 'serialization failure: this transaction
  conflicts with a committed transaction from another client, try restarting
  transaction.')

Dolt is doing the right thing. Concurrent transactions register the same schema row, one commits, the rest are told their transaction conflicted and to restart it. Nothing restarts it, so the exception propagates out of flob.run(), and the whole run is lost: the run-start record as well as the result, because the failure happens inside start() before anything is written.

The loss rate measured here is ~20% of all writes and ~70-80% of the first write per worker, at concurrency 5. bd-auto's default concurrency is 5.

What this is NOT, and the stress test proves it separately: nothing already committed is ever lost. The barrier merging five worker branches loses nothing, tearing down a worktree loses nothing, and killing a worker mid-write costs at most its own run. The store is gitignored and never on a branch, so a merge has nothing to resolve. This failure is loud, not silent — an exception the caller sees, not a record that quietly disappears.

The fix belongs in flob, not bd-auto: retry on error 1213 with a bounded backoff, around the schema registration at minimum and arguably around any write transaction. 1213 is the documented, expected way a serialisable store tells a client to try again.
design:
Do not change bd-auto's concurrency to work around this. A store that cannot take concurrent writers is a store bug, and lowering concurrency hides it while leaving every other concurrent flob user exposed.

The retry belongs at the layer that owns the connection, in flob/store/dolt.py, so every caller gets it rather than each call site remembering. Error 1213 specifically: a serialisation failure is safe to retry by definition, and retrying anything else would paper over real errors.
acceptance_criteria:
- scripts/flob-stress.sh passes all 9 checks with WORKERS=5, and still passes at WORKERS=10.
- The retry is on error 1213 only.
- A test drives two processes registering the same schema simultaneously and asserts both runs land.
notes: Filed from beads-auto-imp-3k2. The evidence is scripts/flob-stress.sh in this repo; the fix is in ~/dev/full-observability, which this session deliberately did not modify.
close_reason:
Fixed in ~/dev/full-observability on branch fix/dolt-serialization-retry, commit 1dbbbd2 (branched off fix/dolt-server-leak, not merged — that is the user's call).

The retry sits where the issue's design said: at the layer that owns the connection in src/flob/store/dolt.py, wrapping query, execute, executemany, script and dolt_commit. Error 1213 only, read from args[0] rather than from the message. Five attempts over ~0.75s of jittered backoff — jitter because five processes that conflicted are five processes retrying, and in step they conflict again. script() retries one statement at a time, not as a whole: under autocommit a conflict on the fourth statement has already committed the first three, and restarting the script would apply them twice.

All three acceptance criteria met:
1. scripts/flob-stress.sh passes all 9 checks at WORKERS=5 (20 writes attempted, 20 recorded — it was 4 of 5 first writes failing) and at WORKERS=10 (40 and 40).
2. The retry is on 1213 only; tests/test_concurrency.py asserts 1062 is raised on the first attempt.
3. tests/test_concurrency.py drives two processes through the same schema registration, released together by a barrier file so neither wins by starting first, and asserts both runs land. It is a real test: with _RETRY_ATTEMPTS set to 1 it fails with exactly the 1213 traceback from this issue.

flob's full suite (393 tests) passes and ruff check is clean. bd-auto's concurrency was not touched, as the design section required.

title: Semantic dedup: a discovery is matched against the backlog by what it says, not by its title string
description:
runstate.Discovery.Key() normalises the title and nothing else, so two reports of one bug dedup only if the two models happened to phrase the title the same way. They do not.

beads-auto-imp-b6m and beads-auto-imp-1p8 are the same race inside .git/worktrees, filed 23 hours apart by two workers. Titles: 'Flaky: concurrent git worktree add fails on another worktree's commondir' and 'Concurrent git worktree add races, and a wave of five can lose an issue to it before any model runs'. Title-normalised matching has no chance. Both sat open until a human read them side by side. The same thing happened with beads-auto-imp-pzi and beads-auto-imp-6up, which beads-auto-imp-fqu cites, and there a whole drain attempt was spent on the duplicate before a worker closed it.

The signal is in the bodies, and it is strong: both worktree issues quote the same error string, 'failed to read .git/worktrees/<name>/commondir', and both name internal/worktree. What distinguishes a duplicate is the rare tokens two issues share — a path, an identifier, an error message — not the common ones. Weight tokens by how rare they are in the backlog and the two match easily, while two issues that merely both say 'worker' and 'issue' do not.
design:
A similarity pass over title plus description, scoring a candidate discovery against every open issue.

Tokenise on non-identifier boundaries but keep dotted paths, slashed paths and mixed-case identifiers whole, since those are the tokens that carry identity. Weight each token by inverse document frequency across the open backlog: a token in most issues is worth nearly nothing, one in a single issue is worth a lot. Score is the weighted overlap of the two token sets over the weight of the smaller set, so a short discovery still matches a long issue that contains it.

Deterministic and offline, so it is testable and costs nothing. No model call: this runs at the barrier where a model call is another thing to fail, and the b6m/1p8 pair is separated by lexical evidence alone.

Threshold is configuration, not a constant, and the default is set by checking it against the pairs this repo already has: b6m/1p8 and pzi/6up must match, and pairs that are merely adjacent must not.

A match does not silently drop the discovery. It is recorded against the issue it duplicates, so triage shows 'looks like <id>' and a human can disagree.
acceptance_criteria:
- Scoring is a pure function over two texts plus a corpus, unit tested with the real b6m/1p8 and pzi/6up text as fixtures, both scoring above threshold.
- At least two near-miss pairs from this backlog score below threshold, so the test proves it discriminates rather than matching everything.
- Rare tokens outweigh common ones: a test where two issues share only common words scores near zero.
- The barrier and triage both consult it before filing, and a matched discovery is recorded with the id it matched and never filed as a new issue.
- Threshold is configurable and validated.
close_reason: internal/similar scores two texts on the rarity-weighted terms they share. Measured by sweeping all 4371 pairs of this repo's real backlog: 6up/pzi, the duplicate that cost a drain attempt, stands alone at 0.63 and is dropped outright; 1p8/b6m sits at 0.32 in a band it shares with epics and their own children, so it is reported to a human rather than resolved. Two thresholds rather than one tuned number, because tuning until that pair passed would fit this backlog and lose real work in the next. Tests found two bugs on the way in: camelCase split after lowercasing, and map-order float summation making scores differ between runs.

title: Triage gate: a discovery is staged for a human, not filed as an issue by the barrier
description:
Measured over this project's whole history, agent-discovered work peaked at 2.27 issues created per issue closed (34 created / 15 closed across the wz9 drains, 19 of the 34 carrying a discovered-from edge). The discovery edges show the shape: nine different parent issues each produced exactly two children (wz9.2, wz9.6, wz9.7, wz9.8, wz9.11, j5a.6, o4q, 908, tv9). Real discovery is lumpy; a constant two per issue is form-filling.

beads-auto-imp-fqu moved filing from the worker to the barrier and beads-auto-imp-qhs put a bar in the prompt, and both helped. What neither changed is that the barrier still runs bd create, so the issue count grows whether or not anything was learned. DiscoveredDefer hides the result from bd ready, which protects the next run, but the backlog a human reads is the thing that actually grows.

Add a third mode to discovered_work: triage. Under it the barrier files nothing. Discoveries accumulate in a durable staging file that outlives the run, and a new command bd-auto triage is what turns one into an issue, folds it into an existing issue as a note, or discards it. Nothing becomes a bd issue until a human says so.
design:
config.DiscoveredWork gains 'triage' alongside defer and immediate, and triage becomes the default: filing an issue is the irreversible half and should be opt-in.

Staging lives at .beads/auto/triage.json, not in run.json, because run state is per-run and a discovery outlives the run that found it. Entries carry title, description, type, priority, the issue and run they were found in, and a resolution once triaged.

bd-auto triage is scriptable rather than only interactive, so a headless operator and a test can both drive it: --list, --accept <key>, --into <issue> for a merge, --discard <key> --reason, and --accept-all. Merge appends to the target issue's notes rather than creating anything.

Three outcomes are kept, not two: a discarded discovery stays in the file with its reason, because the record of what a run decided not to file is the evidence that the bar is set right.
acceptance_criteria:
- discovered_work: triage is accepted by config validation and is the default in a generated config.
- Under triage the barrier files no issues and the staging file holds every discovery the run harvested.
- bd-auto triage --list prints pending discoveries with the issue each was found in.
- --accept files exactly one issue, with the discovered-from edge the barrier used to add.
- --into appends to an existing issue's notes and files nothing.
- --discard records the reason and never offers that discovery again.
- Staging survives a run ending, a new run starting, and bd-auto run stop.
- defer and immediate keep working exactly as they do now.
close_reason: discovered_work: triage is the default and the barrier files nothing. Staging is .beads/auto/triage.json, which outlives the run; bd-auto triage --list/--accept/--into/--discard/--accept-all is the human's half, scriptable so a smoke test can drive it. Fold-into-existing is the shape that was missing. defer and immediate are unchanged and now also consult internal/similar. This repo switched itself to triage.

title: The reviewer role can write issue state, and did: a review ran bd close on the issue under review
description:
From .beads/auto/logs/beads-auto-imp-46o-a1-r0-review.jsonl, the reviewer says: "I mistakenly ran bd close beads-auto-imp-46o and bd update ... --notes=... during this review... reviewers must not touch issue state." beads-auto-imp-46o close_reason is now the literal string "review only, not closing".

A reviewer is meant to return a verdict. It should not be able to close, reopen, comment on or re-note the issue it is judging: a review that mutates the record can close work that never landed, and the engine trusts issue state when it decides what to merge and when an epic settles.

The reviewer already runs under permissions: scoped. The allowlist evidently permits bd writes. Restrict the reviewer to read-only bd (show, list, ready) and deny the mutating verbs, so this is refused by the harness rather than by instructions in a prompt.
acceptance_criteria:
- A reviewer attempting bd close, bd update or bd create is refused by the permission layer, not merely told not to.
- The refusal is reported (see beads-auto-imp-84g) rather than silently weakening the verdict.
- beads-auto-imp-46o close_reason is corrected.
- A test asserts the reviewer allowlist excludes the mutating bd verbs.
notes:
Acceptance criterion 3 (correct beads-auto-imp-46o's close_reason) was not applied. Setting that field needs 'bd close beads-auto-imp-46o --reason=...' — bd update has no flag for it — and this worker's own Claude Code session refused the command (auto-mode classifier, then 'requires approval' with nobody headless to approve). ask_user reported nobody watching the run, so the assumption made was: land the enforcement, the reporting and the tests, and hand the one-line correction to a human rather than reach for bd sql. The command is: bd close beads-auto-imp-46o --reason="merge-order asks the integrator instead of guessing (877b169)". Also: the reporting half of this issue overlaps beads-auto-imp-84g, which is now implemented (refused tools go to the run log and a '- refused:' line in .beads/auto/review/<id>.md).
Round 2: acceptance criterion 3 is now applied. 'bd close beads-auto-imp-46o --reason="merge-order asks the integrator instead of guessing (877b169)"' was refused by this session's harness in round 1 and went through unchanged in round 2; bd show beads-auto-imp-46o now reports that reason. The earlier note about handing the command to a human is superseded, and the discovery filed for it has been withdrawn.
close_reason: Closed

title: scope.Blocked never checks whether the scoped issue is itself deferred
description:
internal/drain/scope.go:326-345 walks an issue dependencies to decide if it is blocked, but never asks whether the issue itself carries a deferral. beads-auto-imp-j5a.2 fixed Candidates and candidateSet, so a deferred issue no longer enters a scope preview — but an issue named explicitly in --issues bypasses that path. parkOutOfScope therefore cannot catch it: the issue sits unready for the whole run and falls to the end-of-run sweep.

This is what produced drain 5 seventeen stranded issues. It is the real bug behind the note that reads "never became ready, and the run drained without bd ever offering it".
acceptance_criteria:
- scope.Blocked reports a deferred issue as blocked, naming its own deferral rather than a dependency.
- An explicitly scoped deferred issue is refused or parked at scope time, before any worktree is created.
- A test covers an issue deferred in its own right, distinct from one blocked by a deferred dependency.
close_reason: Closed

title: Test run: stress flob (refs/dolt/flob) across drain worktrees and prove no records are lost
description:
The drain test run and scripts/smoke.sh exercise the beads Dolt store only. flob (~/dev/full-observability) is a second Dolt-backed tool that travels on the git remote under refs/dolt/flob, a ref it took deliberately so it can sit beside the beads ref refs/dolt/data (see src/flob/store/dolt.py DATA_REF and src/flob/cli/sync_cmd.py).

A bd-auto drain runs N worker worktrees off one checkout and merges them at a barrier, so every hazard beads has already hit applies to flob as well, over data that is far more expensive to lose: flob records experiment runs, and a dropped record costs the training time that produced it.

Extend the test run to cover a repo where flob is initialised and being written while a drain is in flight. Workers record flob runs concurrently, the integrator merges their branches, and the test then proves every record written is still readable and that refs/dolt/flob advanced without losing a Dolt commit.

Hazards to cover explicitly:
- a barrier merge that resolves refs/dolt/flob by taking one side, silently dropping the other side records. The beads analogue is beads-auto-imp-xdv, where every branch in a wave carries a full export of one shared database.
- worktree teardown or gitguard removing or rewinding a flob store a worker has just written.
- two workers running flob push against the same ref inside one wave.
- a gate failure, a peel-back or a retry that resets a branch and takes flob commits with it.

SAFETY, and this is the point of the issue: the test must build its own throwaway repo and its own flob store, the way scripts/resume-vs-fresh.sh already builds a fixture repo. It must never run against ~/dev/full-observability or any other real flob store. Records there are not reproducible without paying for the training that produced them again.
design:
Depends on beads-auto-imp-xdv: xdv decides how a shared Dolt-backed store is kept out of per-worker commits, and whatever mechanism it lands (pre-commit unstage, integrator regeneration, or dropping the hook chain in worktrees) is what this test has to exercise for a second store on a second ref. Building the flob case before xdv lands would test a shape that is about to change.

Prefer extending scripts/smoke.sh (see beads-auto-imp-tpk, which adds the drain case with provider: fake) over a new harness, so there is one end-to-end script. provider: fake keeps the cost at zero while still driving real worktrees, real commits and a real barrier.
acceptance_criteria:
- The test builds an isolated fixture repo with its own flob init and its own Dolt store, and touches no store outside that fixture. A guard fails the test if the working store resolves anywhere near a real one.
- A drain over that fixture writes flob records from at least 3 concurrent workers.
- After integration every record written by every worker is readable through flob query, and the count matches exactly what was written.
- refs/dolt/flob after the barrier contains every Dolt commit made by every worker, none dropped by a merge resolution.
- Killing one worker mid-write leaves every other worker records intact.
- Loss is reported as which records went missing, not only as a count mismatch.
notes: Filed at the request of the repo owner alongside drain 5. flob is at ~/dev/full-observability, currently on branch fix/dolt-server-leak. Its own recent commits (874919c sync: give flob a ref of its own; 38650c8 store: stop the Dolt server a reproduction and a test leave behind) show the same class of problem being fixed on that side.
close_reason: implemented and merged on main in PR #3; reopened by a post-checkout hook importing a stale .beads/issues.jsonl, not by any decision

title: Concurrent `git worktree add` races, and a wave of five can lose an issue to it before any model runs
description:
internal/worktree/worktree.go Ensure/Create runs `git worktree add` with no serialisation, and drain_wave.go dispatches one per issue concurrently — the comment at worktree.go:100 already notes that 'a wave runs several Ensure calls at once'. Concurrent adds race inside .git/worktrees: git fails with `fatal: failed to read .git/worktrees/<other-issue>/commondir: Success` while another add is mid-write.

Reproduced on a585bf5 with no changes applied: `go test ./internal/drain/ -count=12` failed TestDrainRunsADagAcrossWavesAndParksWhatFailed twice with that error, and TestAnOutageStopsTheWaveWithoutParkingAnything once on a separate run. It only shows under load — the tests pass 120/120 when run alone — which is why it reads as an unrelated flake rather than what it is.

It is not only a test flake. The engine reports the failure as `worktree: create ...` from Engine.Issue, which is a returned error rather than an outcome, so the whole Drain call fails and takes its siblings with it. concurrency defaults to 5, so a real run makes five of these calls at once against the same repository.

A fix has to serialise worktree creation across a wave — a mutex in internal/worktree around the add, or a queue in the dispatcher — and cover it with a test that creates several worktrees concurrently and asserts they all land.

Found by the bd-auto worker on beads-auto-imp-j5a.6, and filed at the wave barrier — deferred, so it waits for a human rather than being offered to the next run.
close_reason: closed on main in PR #3 (1p8: already fixed when filed; txg: measured, and the answer is not to build it); reopened by a post-checkout hook importing a stale .beads/issues.jsonl, not by any decision

title: A worker that parks itself is recorded done and merged, because Terminal() treats blocked as finished
description:
prompts/worker.md step 7 tells a worker that cannot finish to run:

    bd update <issue-id> --status=blocked --append-notes="bd-auto attempt: <what blocked you>"

The engine then reads that as success.

internal/drain/issue.go:261 checks 'if !cur.Terminal()', and bd.Issue.Terminal() is Closed() || Blocked() (internal/bd/bd.go:64). A blocked issue passes. The attempt goes on to the git guard and the review stages and, if they pass, returns OutcomeDone (issue.go:290) — so recordDone marks it done, its branch is merged at the barrier, and the run reports it as completed work.

It gets worse at the barrier. reconcile() (internal/drain/reconcile.go:82) walks st.Done, sees bd has the issue blocked rather than closed, and re-closes it with a reason blaming beads' post-checkout hook for reverting a write that was never reverted — the worker set that status deliberately. The one signal the worker had to say 'I could not do this' is overwritten with a sentence saying the tracker lost an update.

This is how a worker's 'I am blocked by something else' turns into a green run. It is the mechanism behind the report that motivated this epic: a worker declared its issue out of scope until another issue finished, and the run did not treat that as a park.

Terminal() is right for the places that ask 'may a worker stop here' — parkOutOfScope and parkStranded both use it to mean 'already settled'. It is wrong as the completion test for an attempt.
design:
Split the check at internal/drain/issue.go:261. Closed means done and continues to the stages. Blocked means the worker parked itself: stop the attempt there and return an outcome that says so, carrying the worker's own note as the reason so a human reads what the worker wrote rather than a generic 'attempts exhausted'.

Decide, and record the decision in the issue's notes, whether a self-park costs an attempt. It should not: retrying a worker that told you it is blocked buys another identical answer at full price. Treat it as terminal for the issue and park it immediately with the worker's reason.

Nothing should merge. A self-parked issue's branch must not land at the barrier — check how MergeParked is reached from a report whose outcome is parked (internal/drain/integrate.go) and make sure this path takes it.

reconcile() must be left alone. It re-asserts the run's own record, and once the run's record says parked it will re-park rather than re-close, which is the correct behaviour and needs no special case.
acceptance_criteria: A worker that sets --status=blocked ends the issue as parked with the worker's own note as the reason, not done. Its branch is not merged. Run state records it in Parked, so the barrier's reconcile re-parks rather than re-closes it. The self-park does not consume the remaining attempts. Tests cover: blocked at the end of round 1, blocked after a passing gate, and closed-then-blocked ordering. Existing tests that rely on Terminal() as the completion test are updated rather than deleted.
notes:
Found while investigating the report that motivated beads-auto-imp-j5a.4 — a worker calling a sibling in its own wave a blocker. What happens after such a declaration is this bug.
Decision (asked for in the design): a self-park does NOT cost an attempt, and it is terminal for the issue. A worker that has read the issue and concluded it cannot do the work is answering the question, not failing to answer it; a fresh worker on attempt 2 reads the same issue and reaches the same conclusion, at full price. So the attempt returns OutcomeBlocked, Issue() parks immediately with the worker's own reason, and the remaining attempts are left unspent. bd.Park is still called — bd already has the status, but the human label is how bd human list finds a parked issue.

Also decided: the blocked check sits ABOVE the progress check, not below it. A worker that cannot do the work usually has nothing to commit, so the round that says so is a round that changed nothing, and the progress check would have failed the attempt and bought the retry this is meant to avoid. It is safe there for the reason the progress check exists: a blocked status is not satisfiable by the previous round's state, because it ends the attempt the moment it is seen rather than buying another round on it.
Gate round 2: the gate failed on TestAParkedIssueOpensNoPullRequest with 'git worktree add ... fatal: failed to read .git/worktrees/t-1/commondir'. Measured, not guessed: the base commit a585bf5 fails that test about 3 times in 300 runs and this branch's change fails it 0 in 300, so the flake is pre-existing and nothing to do with the blocked check. It is a real race in internal/worktree though — a wave dispatches its workers at once and every one starts with git worktree add, git scans .git/worktrees/ as it adds, and a second add that catches a half-written entry dies. Fixed rather than filed, because it is what failed the gate and it costs a real run an issue for a reason no human can act on: a package-level mutex now serialises every registry operation (Ensure, Prune, Remove, List, Entries), with unlocked internals so nothing re-enters. Out of this issue's scope, and said so in the final message.
close_reason: Closed

title: Deferred issues are counted as workable: they enter scope previews, block epic closure and inflate run status
description:
bd's list and stats do not subtract deferred work, and bd-auto believes them.

Measured in this repo today:

    bd list --json --limit 0   -> 19 open, 16 of them with defer_until in 2029
    bd stats                   -> Open: 19, Ready to Work: 19
    bd ready --json            -> 2

So 'Ready to Work: 19' is wrong by 17. bd-auto manufactures these itself: discovered work is filed deferred at +1000d (DiscoveredDefer, internal/drain/discover.go:209), which is the right call — it keeps discovered work out of the run a human approved — but it means every run leaves behind issues that later runs then mistake for work.

Where it lands:

- internal/bd/bd.go:158 Children() runs 'bd list --parent --all --limit 0 --flat' and gets the deferred children back. scope.Candidates (internal/scope/scope.go:95) skips only closed and blocked ones, so a deferred child is offered to the human as something to scope a run to. Pick it and bd ready never offers it, the planner never dispatches it, and parkStranded parks it at the end of the run with 'never became ready, and the run drained without bd ever offering it' (internal/drain/drain_wave.go:702) — true, and no help at all.
- EpicComplete (internal/drain/integrate.go:755) counts any unclosed child as open. A deferred child therefore lands in v.Open and, being outside the scope, in v.OutOfScope, so the epic can never close and the reason a human reads names issues nobody can work.
- EpicStats (internal/bd/bd.go:319) counts them Open, so 'bd-auto run status' (internal/cmds/run.go:205) reports work that is hidden from bd ready by construction.
- scope.Blocked (internal/scope/scope.go:273) parks an in-scope issue whose blocker is out of scope. It does not consider a blocker that is IN scope but deferred, which can never become ready either.

bd.Issue (internal/bd/bd.go:38) has no defer_until field at all, so none of this code can currently tell the difference.
design:
Add DeferUntil time.Time `json:"defer_until"` to bd.Issue, and a Deferred(now time.Time) bool helper beside Closed()/Blocked()/Terminal(). Take the clock as an argument rather than calling time.Now inside it, so tests are not date-dependent.

Then treat deferred as not-actionable at each site:

- scope.Candidates: skip with Skipped[id] = "deferred until <date>", so the preview still accounts for every child rather than silently showing a shorter list.
- scope.Blocked: an in-scope blocker that is deferred can never become ready, so report it with that reason rather than waiting for parkStranded to say nothing useful.
- EpicComplete: do not count a deferred child as open. Name them separately in the reason ('N deferred child issue(s) are not in this run's way') so a human can see why the epic closed over unclosed children.
- bd.Stats: a Deferred count of its own, and run status showing it.

Do NOT filter deferred issues out of bd.Client.All() (internal/bd/bd.go:171). That is what discovery deduplication is checked against, and a deferred issue is exactly the kind a worker will rediscover — dropping it would refile it every run.

This is a workaround for bd's behaviour, not a fix to bd. Say so in a comment where the workaround lives, with the numbers above, so nobody later 'simplifies' it back out.
acceptance_criteria: A deferred child never appears as a scope candidate and is accounted for in Skipped. An epic whose only remaining unclosed children are deferred closes, with a reason that names them. bd-auto run status reports deferred work separately from open work. An in-scope issue whose only blocker is deferred is parked before dispatch with that reason rather than stranded at the end. bd.Client.All() still returns deferred issues. Tests use a synthetic issue with defer_until in the future and an injected clock.
close_reason: defer_until now on bd.Issue/bd.Ref with a Deferred(now) helper; deferred children are skipped from scope candidates and accounted for in Skipped, refused when named explicitly, reported by scope.Blocked as an in-scope blocker with its own fix, excluded from EpicComplete's open count and named in the reason, and counted separately by bd.Stats and run status. All() still returns them, pinned by a test. Gate green.

title: bd-auto: a transcript view, deferred-issue blindness, and wave slots that refill
description:
Three things a live drain does badly, plus two defects found while confirming them.

1. The wave table shows one line per issue and nothing else. There is no way to see what a worker actually did — the transcripts are on disk at .beads/auto/logs/ and invisible from the view that is watching them stream past.

2. bd's own list and stats count deferred work as open and ready. bd-auto manufactures deferred issues itself (discover.go files discovered work at +1000d), so every run poisons its own later runs: deferred children become scope candidates, block epic closure, and inflate run status.

3. A wave is planned at exactly the concurrency cap and never grows. An issue that parks in the first minute leaves its worker slot idle until the barrier, while in-scope issues sit in the table saying 'waiting'.

Found while confirming (2) and (3): a worker that does what prompts/worker.md step 7 tells it to do when blocked is recorded as done and merged, and nothing in the run or the prompt tells a worker that a sibling running beside it is not a blocker.
acceptance_criteria: All five children closed: the detail view ships with screenshots, deferred issues are excluded from every actionable path, a blocked worker is never recorded done, the worker prompt covers siblings, and a freed slot is refilled before the barrier.
close_reason: All 7 children closed across drains 5 and 7: transcript detail view, deferred-issue blindness, self-parking workers recorded done, sibling-is-not-a-blocker, slot refill, per-role status, and the barrier row. Acceptance criteria met.

title: The barrier is invisible: a model resolving a conflict shows as an idle table
description:
Drain 3 put two workers on the same function on purpose. Both finished, the barrier could not merge the second branch, and bd-auto spawned an integrator to resolve it — a model call that ran for minutes and cost real money.

For all of that the live view said:

    0 running · 2 done · 0 parked · 0 killed · run total $2.5144
    ↑/↓ select · k kill the selected worker · q stop the run

Nothing about a barrier, nothing about a conflict, nothing about a model in flight. A watcher cannot tell a run that is integrating from a run that has hung, which is the one distinction the display exists to make — the same argument the row's own activity column is built on.

The engine knows: it merges in order, it logs '<issue>: <branch> conflicts in <paths>', and the integrator streams events like any other process. The bus has no event for the barrier opening, so the view cannot say so. It needs one: a wave-integrating event when merging starts, and the integrator's activity routed to the row of the issue whose branch it is resolving.
acceptance_criteria: A barrier that starts merging says so in the status line, an integrator's activity appears against the issue it is merging, and both are covered by a model test; the deterministic screenshot harness gains a scene for it.
close_reason: new EventWaveIntegrating opens the barrier on the status line and the integrator's activity is tagged with the issue whose branch it is resolving; TestTheBarrierSaysItIsWorking and TestTheBarrierAnnouncesItselfAndTagsTheIntegrator, plus the tui-08-integrating screenshot

title: A row parked by the barrier keeps saying done, and the counters keep counting it
description:
Drain 2's last leg ended with the table saying '1 done · 0 parked' directly above the run's own verdict, 'run done after 1 wave(s): 3 done, 1 parked'. The issue in question, kv-555.4, had finished its worker and then been parked at integration because the merge refused: its work did not land.

The view learns this. EventWaveEnd carries the whole IntegrateReport, and the model uses it for one thing only — a status line saying how many merged and how many parked. The rows are never touched, so an issue the barrier parked keeps the state its worker left it in, and every counter derived from the rows keeps counting it as done.

A row should follow the barrier's verdict: an issue in Integration.Parked() becomes parked, with the merge's reason as its activity, so the table and the run agree.
acceptance_criteria: EventWaveEnd flips each parked merge's row to parked with the reason as its detail, and leaves merged rows alone; a model test drives a wave-end with one merged and one parked issue and asserts both rows and the counter line.
close_reason: EventWaveEnd now moves a done row the barrier parked to parked, with the merge reason as its activity, and leaves killed or failed rows alone; TestTheBarrierMovesTheRowsItParked

title: every wave is reported one lower than it is, so the first wave has no number at all
description:
The drain loop loads run state, plans a wave, and then emits EventWaveStart, EventIssueStart and EventIssueEnd with st.Wave from the copy it loaded. But the thing that advances the wave counter is wave.Record, which writes it to disk and returns the updated state — and nextWave throws that return value away. So the caller's st.Wave is still the number of the wave before this one.

The first wave is therefore emitted as wave 0, which the table renders as a dash in the WAVE column and drops from the heading entirely, and the second as wave 1. The barrier does not share the fault: Integrate reloads run state, so EventWaveEnd carries the real number — which means one screen says 'wave 0' in every row while the status line under it says 'wave 1 integrated'.

Seen in the live kv-ctf drain: three issues, two waves, and the WAVE column read '-' throughout.
acceptance_criteria: The first wave is emitted as 1; the wave a row shows agrees with the wave the barrier reports for it; a test drives a two-wave drain and asserts on the numbers in the events.

title: flob leaks a detached dolt sql-server per repro run and per untorn-down test project
description:
244 orphaned 'dolt sql-server' processes accumulated on this machine (~6.3 GB RSS, oldest 3 days), all reparented to systemd --user. Source is flob (~/dev/full-observability), not beads.

DoltStore.start() (src/flob/store/dolt.py:230) spawns the server with start_new_session=True, deliberately detached so it outlives the CLI. close() explicitly keeps the server running. There is no atexit hook, no finalizer, and no idle timeout, so only an explicit DoltStore.stop() ever reaps a server. Three paths create stores and never call it:

1. flob repro (125 leaks). repro.py:153 mkdtemps a /tmp/flob-repro-* worktree; _prepare_scratch (repro.py:284) gives it a fresh .flob/dolt; the child re-run starts a detached server there. The finally block calls _remove_worktree (repro.py:235) which does git worktree remove + rmtree + prune, but never stops the server. One leak per invocation, each left pinned to a deleted directory.

2. Test suite (111 leaks). conftest.py:96 stops the server, but only on the 'project' fixture. Six tests bypass it and leak once per pytest run: test_cli.py:52,72,97,124 (bare 'repo' fixture then flob init), test_sdk.py:452 (project built under tmp_path), and test_cli.py:440 (uses 'project', but also creates a second project at tmp_path/other which is never stopped). test_sync.py already patches this per-call-site in three places, which is the same bug being fixed one site at a time.

3. Git worktrees (6 leaks). theological-LLMs/.claude/worktrees/agent-*/.flob/dolt servers outlived their worktrees, which were removed after merge.

The 242 leaked processes have been killed; the 2 live project stores were left running.
design: Keep the detached-server design: it is correct for a user running 'flob ls' twice, and the Ctrl-C-mid-write rationale at dolt.py:226-228 still holds. Fix the ownership gaps rather than making the server die with its parent. The scratch store in repro is process-owned and short-lived, so it is the one case that should always be torn down explicitly.
acceptance_criteria:
- _remove_worktree stops the scratch store's dolt server before deleting the worktree, so 'flob repro' leaves no server behind
- Test teardown reaps any dolt server started under tmp_path, not just the one owned by the 'project' fixture; the per-call-site stop() calls in test_sync.py become redundant
- A full pytest run leaves zero 'dolt sql-server' processes behind
- A backstop exists for servers whose --data-dir no longer exists (gc command or server-side timeout)
notes:
Fixed in full-observability@38650c8 on branch fix/dolt-server-leak (pushed; main fast-forwarded to 9d03208 and pushed first).

Three changes:
1. repro.py — _stop_scratch(scratch) in the finally block, before _remove_worktree, since stop() reads the pid file from inside the worktree.
2. tests/conftest.py — autouse _reap_dolt_servers fixture reaps by the pid file under tmp_path, replacing the project-fixture-only teardown; the three trailing DoltStore(other).stop() lines in test_sync.py removed as redundant (they also never ran when a test failed partway).
3. store/dolt.py + cli/main.py — running_servers()/stray_servers()/reap() and a 'flob servers [--reap]' command as the backstop for worktrees removed by something other than flob. The data dir is sliced out of the raw ps line rather than split on whitespace: a truncated path would not exist on disk, so a live store's server would have been read as stray and killed.

A full suite run now leaves 0 servers behind, was 6 per run plus one per repro execution. test_a_reproduction_leaves_no_dolt_server_behind confirmed to fail with the fix reverted. title: bd-auto hook: a missing subcommand wedges a whole Claude Code session, tools and turn-end alike
description:
A Claude Code session in this repo registers two hooks that point at a
subcommand bd-auto does not have:

    "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}"/bin/bd-auto hook pre-tool-use
    "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}"/bin/bd-auto hook stop

bd-auto has no `hook` command, so it prints its usage and exits non-zero.
Claude Code reads that exit as "block", and the result is a session that
cannot do anything:

- PreToolUse: EVERY Bash call is refused before it runs. Not a class of
  commands — every one, `true` included. git, go, bd: all unreachable.
- Stop: every attempt to end a turn is refused, so the model is re-invoked
  immediately, forever.

Observed for real, not hypothesised. The session that hit this burned
roughly forty turns alternating "still blocked" and "idle" before Claude
Code's own backstop fired: "A hook blocked the turn from ending 9
consecutive times - overriding and ending turn." Until that cap, the loop
was unbounded and self-sustaining: the agent could neither act nor stop,
and could not fix the hook, because fixing it needs the shell the hook is
blocking. The only escape found was the Monitor tool, which runs commands
in the same shell but is not covered by the hook's matcher. That is a hole
in the sandbox, not a supported route, and it should not be the thing
standing between a wedged session and its work.

Where the config lives is itself part of the bug: it is nowhere. Searching
~/.claude, ~/dev and ~/.config for "hook pre-tool-use" and for
CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT turns up only conversation transcripts - no
hooks.json, no settings entry, and .claude-plugin/plugin.json declares no
hooks at all. The hooks were loaded into a running session from config
that has since been removed, and they persist in that session's memory
until it restarts. So the operator's fix is "restart Claude Code", which is
not discoverable from the error, and there is no file to edit.

This is bd-auto's problem to prevent, whatever put the config there. We
ship the plugin, and a plugin whose hook can wedge a session has to fail
open. A hook is on the path of every single tool call; it is the one place
in the system where exiting non-zero on an unrecognised input costs the
user their whole session.
design:
Fail open, in this order:

1. `bd-auto hook <event>` must exist and must exit 0 for ANY event name,
   including ones it does nothing with. An unknown event is a version skew
   between the shipped hooks config and the shipped binary - the normal
   consequence of upgrading one and not the other - and the correct
   response to it is to do nothing quietly, not to take the session down.
   This is the opposite of the rule everywhere else in bd-auto, where an
   unknown subcommand is a typo worth refusing. On the hook path the cost
   is not symmetric.

2. Honour `stop_hook_active`. Claude Code puts it in the Stop hook's stdin
   JSON precisely so a hook cannot trap a session: when it is true the hook
   must return success immediately. Any Stop hook we ship reads it first.
   Without this, a Stop hook that blocks blocks forever - the model is
   re-invoked, tries to stop, is blocked again.

3. Never let the exit code carry an argument-parsing failure. Usage errors
   from a `hook` invocation go to stderr and exit 0; only a genuine,
   deliberate block exits 2.

4. If we ship hooks config, ship it with the binary that satisfies it, and
   have the hook itself no-op when it cannot find its own version. The
   failure mode to design against is not "someone wrote a bad config" but
   "the two halves moved independently", which is the ordinary state of a
   repo where a plugin is built from the tree it configures.

Worth deciding separately: whether bd-auto should register PreToolUse at
all. Every call it sees costs a process spawn, and it is the blast radius
of exactly this bug.
acceptance_criteria: 1. `bd-auto hook <anything>` exits 0 and is silent on stdout for any event name, known or not. 2. A Stop hook payload with stop_hook_active=true returns success without doing work. 3. A regression test runs the shipped hooks config against the shipped binary for every event it registers and asserts exit 0. 4. Reproduced first: point a PreToolUse hook at a nonexistent bd-auto subcommand, confirm every Bash call is refused, then confirm the fix clears it.
notes:
Reproduced before fixing, at the exit code Claude Code acts on.

Built the tree at HEAD into a scratch checkout and ran the two commands from
the report against it:

  bd-auto hook pre-tool-use -> exit 2
  bd-auto hook stop         -> exit 2

Exit 2 is Claude Code's block code, so that is one refusal per tool call and
one per turn end, which is the session the report describes. Against the fixed
binary both come back 0.

The reported hooks config was then written to .claude/settings.local.json and
run through the new regression test. It fails, and on the arm that matters: the
commands survive the built binary but exit 127 when bd-auto is absent, which is
version skew in the other direction. That is why the shipped-config test has
two arms and why a shipped hook command has to carry its own '|| true'.
close_reason: bd-auto hook exists and fails open; regression tests hold the binary and any shipped hooks config to it

title: Discoveries are filed by bd-auto at the barrier, not by the worker
description:
A worker filing its own discovered work with 'bd create' has two problems. It has no view of what any other worker filed, so the same finding lands twice — beads-auto-imp-pzi and beads-auto-imp-6up are the same work filed by two workers three waves apart. And the create is a bd write from inside a worktree, which is exactly the class of write beads-auto-imp-g7t says does not survive a checkout-shaped git operation.

Move the filing to bd-auto. The worker writes what it found to .beads/auto/discovered.json in its worktree (gitignored, so 'git add -A' cannot commit it); bd-auto harvests that file at the end of every attempt into run state, and files the issues itself at the barrier, deduplicated by normalised title against both what this run already filed and every issue already in bd.
acceptance_criteria: Worker prompt step 6 writes a file rather than running bd create. Engine harvests it per attempt into run state. Barrier files each unfiled discovery once, deduped against run state and against bd. Duplicate titles are recorded as skipped rather than filed twice.

title: ask_user MCP tool: let a headless worker ask the human a question without ending its session
description:
A headless worker that hits a genuine ambiguity has no way to ask. Today its only options are to guess, or to fail the attempt and let the failure text reach a human on the next round — both expensive and both lossy. Meanwhile the interactive orchestrator path CAN ask, and that turned out to be one of the more valuable things it did.

Give the headless engine the same ability, as a tool rather than as a session exit.

Why a tool specifically: exiting the 'claude -p' process to ask means the next attempt is a new session that must be re-sent the whole context, which is exactly the cost this project exists to avoid. A tool call blocks inside the live session, so the answer costs one tool round-trip instead of a session restart.

Shape:
- bd-auto exposes an MCP server (stdio) offering an ask_user tool, passed to the backend at spawn — for the claude adapter that is --mcp-config plus the tool on the allowlist. The Runner seam already exists, so this must not be claude-specific in the engine; a backend that cannot offer tools should degrade, not break.
- The tool takes a question and a small list of options, matching the shape the Claude Code AskUserQuestion tool uses, since that shape is already proven and models already know it.
- A call blocks the calling worker only. Other workers keep running.
- bd-auto raises the question on the existing drain.Bus; the TUI from beads-auto-imp-wz9.10 renders it as a popup over the wave view and sends the answer back as the tool result.
- Several workers may ask at once. The TUI needs a queue and must make clear which issue is asking; the wave view already has a per-issue row to hang that off.

The hard part is the unattended case, and it is what will make or break this:
- --quiet, --plain, --json and any non-TTY run have nobody to answer. A question must never hang a drain forever.
- Needs an explicit policy with a safe default. Suggested default: answer unavailable, the tool returns promptly telling the model to proceed on its best judgement and record the assumption in the issue, so an unattended drain degrades to today's behaviour rather than stalling.
- A timeout is needed even WITH a TTY, since the human may walk away.
- Questions and answers must be recorded in run state, so a resumed run does not re-ask what was already answered, and so a human reading the run afterwards can see what was decided and why.
design:
Builds on three things already in main: the Runner/Request seam (beads-auto-imp-wz9.1), the drain event bus (beads-auto-imp-wz9.9) and the TUI wave view (beads-auto-imp-wz9.10), which already owns the terminal and already has per-issue rows and working input handling for its kill/stop controls. The MCP server is new; everything it needs to display and answer already exists.

Open questions for the implementer: whether the server is one per run or one per worker; how the tool is scoped so a worker cannot ask its way around the permission model; whether the reviewer role gets it at all, given it is read-only and judging someone else's work; and how a blocked worker is shown in the wave view so it does not read as hung.
acceptance_criteria:
- A worker under 'claude -p' can call ask_user and receive an answer without its session ending.
- The question appears in the TUI over the wave view, names the asking issue, and the answer returns to that worker as the tool result.
- Other workers continue running while one is blocked.
- Concurrent questions queue rather than fighting over the terminal.
- Non-TTY, --quiet, --plain and --json never hang: the tool returns promptly with the no-human answer and the model is told to proceed and record its assumption.
- A question times out even with a TTY.
- Questions and answers are persisted in run state and survive a resume without being re-asked.
- The engine stays backend-agnostic: nothing claude-specific above the Runner seam.
close_reason: Closed

title: Epic branch + PR handoff: merge a run into a temp branch and open a PR for human review
description:
Today a drain merges each completed issue branch straight into the base branch (main), so a run publishes itself with no human gate. Change the default so a run is staged on a temporary epic branch and handed to a human as a PR.

Behaviour:
- By default, a run over an epic (or any issue set) merges each issue branch, in dependency order, into a temporary epic branch rather than into the base branch.
- Conflicts during those merges use the model, exactly as the existing integrator does — the conflict-only role, resolve-and-stage.
- Only once every issue has merged cleanly and the gate passes on the fully merged epic branch is a PR opened against the base branch.
- The PR is the handoff point: a human reviews and merges. bd-auto never merges to base itself in this mode.
- If any issue is parked, or the gate is red on the epic branch, no PR is opened; the epic branch is left in place for inspection.

Configuration:
- On by default.
- The PR step can be turned off, in which case the epic branch is still produced and left for the human to do what they want with. Decide whether the branch-vs-base-merge behaviour is a separate switch from the PR switch.
design: Builds on internal/drain/integrate.go from beads-auto-imp-wz9.8, which already owns dependency-ordered merges, one model spawn per real conflict, one gate run on the merged result, and cleanup. The change is where the merges land (temp epic branch, not base) plus a terminal PR step. Naming for the temp branch and the PR body (issues landed, gate result, anything discovered) both need deciding. gh CLI is the obvious PR mechanism; note that pushing the epic branch is a publishing action, so it must be reconciled with the gitguard push blocks from beads-auto-imp-wz9.5.
acceptance_criteria:
- Default run merges into a temp epic branch, never into base.
- Merge order is the dependency order; conflicts invoke the model.
- PR is opened only when every issue merged clean AND the gate passed on the epic branch.
- Parked issue or red gate means no PR, epic branch preserved.
- PR step is switchable off, with the epic branch still produced.
- Tests cover: clean run opens a PR, red gate opens none, parked issue opens none, PR disabled produces the branch only.
notes:
Design decision on the switch question, resolved as two switches rather than one.

handoff.branch and handoff.pr are independent, and only in one direction:

  branch: true,  pr: true   (default)  stage on a temp epic branch, then open a PR
  branch: true,  pr: false             stage on the branch, open nothing
  branch: false, pr: false             merge straight into the base branch, as before
  branch: false, pr: true              refused at config load

Why: the two answer different questions. 'branch' is may bd-auto write to the branch you work on; 'pr' is may bd-auto publish. A repo with no remote, no gh, or a review that happens somewhere other than a forge wants the first without the second, and for it the epic branch IS the deliverable — so turning the PR off must still produce it, which is what the user's phrasing asked for and what the acceptance criteria require. The reverse is not a setting but a contradiction: a pull request needs a head branch that is not the base, so pr: true with branch: false is refused at load rather than silently resolved either way. branch: false stays as the escape hatch back to the old behaviour and turns the PR off with it. CLI equivalents are --no-pr and --no-epic-branch.

Two further calls worth recording:

- The PR is a whole-run step, not a per-barrier one. 'Only once every issue has merged cleanly' is a fact about the run, so it lives at the end of the drain (Engine.Handoff, called from finish, the run's single exit) rather than in Integrate. bd-auto integrate therefore stages and merges but never opens a PR.
- The checkout stays on the epic branch for the whole run and is left there. A worker branches from the main checkout HEAD, so moving it back between waves would hand wave two a tree with wave one missing. Switching back at the end is not attempted either: by then the tree holds the whole run and the switch would usually be refused.
