title: Scope selection and bd-auto drain
description:
The human bound on a run, and the wave engine that respects it.

drain does not drain an epic, it drains a set of issues a human named. There is
no automatic limit on spend anywhere in this design, so the bound is applied up
front, at the only moment the user can see what they are agreeing to.

- On a TTY: compute the candidate set (the epic's open, unparked children), show
  it with the wave decomposition, the gate commands and the model chosen per
  role, and require an explicit multi-select and confirmation. Nothing spawns
  before the confirm. It is a preview of the shape of the spend, not a yes/no.
- Off a TTY (skill launcher, CI, --plain): scope must be explicit, via
  --issues a,b,c or --epic X --all. A bare --epic X with no TTY and no explicit
  selection prints the candidate set and EXITS NON-ZERO without dispatching. The
  background path is the one with nobody watching, so it is the one that must
  name its work.
- Selected IDs go to run state as Scope before anything runs. wave.Plan
  intersects bd ready with Scope; an issue outside it is never dispatched,
  whatever bd says about its readiness.
- Discovered work is out of scope by construction: workers file it deferred, and
  a deferred issue was not in the approved list.
- An in-scope issue whose dependency is out of scope and unmet is parked
  immediately with that reason, rather than sitting unready until the run ends
  unable to explain itself.
- The run ends when every scoped issue is done or parked. The epic may still be
  open, and epicComplete refuses to close it unless every child completed.

Then the engine around it: wave loop, errgroup bounded by concurrency, event
bus, plain and --json renderers, and interrupt recovery (resume the persisted
session when the worktree survived, else fresh; attempt counter unchanged
either way).

autonomy shrinks to auto | wave. wave still pauses at each barrier and waits for
bd-auto run resume, which is useful when the scope is large. issue is deleted:
pausing after each issue is redundant when the human already chose the issues.

Interrupt recovery has one known hazard, and it is specific. A claude -p killed
mid-turn can leave a transcript ending in a tool_use block with no matching
tool_result; resuming that sends an invalid message sequence and errors
immediately. With the Class taxonomy that is an infra-failed on the first
resumed turn, which falls back to a fresh dispatch automatically. That is what
makes the least-tested path in the system self-healing rather than a coin flip.
acceptance_criteria:
- An issue outside Scope is never dispatched even when bd ready offers it.
- An in-scope issue with an unmet out-of-scope dependency parks immediately with
  that reason.
- A non-TTY drain with no explicit scope exits non-zero and spawns nothing.
- A 4-issue synthetic DAG in a temp repo with provider: fake exercises a clean
  pass, a parked issue and a full wave barrier.
- Interrupting mid-wave and re-running resumes the interrupted session; a
  resumed first turn returning infra-failed falls back to fresh without
  consuming an attempt.
- Plain and --json renderers cover everything the TUI will show.
close_reason: Closed

title: Measure resume vs fresh, then set the defaults
description:
The recovery design rests on a number nobody has measured yet, so measure it
before choosing the default rather than after.

The claim is that resuming is cheaper than a fresh worker because a fresh worker
re-reads the issue, re-explores the code and re-derives its plan first. The
counterargument, stated honestly in the plan: a resumed session re-sends its
whole transcript every turn, so its per-turn input is strictly larger. The
cache-warmth that would offset this depends on a five-minute TTL, and between
rounds we run the full gate (go build && go vet && go test) and possibly a
reviewer, which can comfortably exceed it. The transcript also grows every round
until it autocompacts, at which point the warm prefix is gone and a compaction
has been paid for.

Drain the same small epic twice with bd-auto issue run:
  max_rounds: 1, retry: 3   (fresh-heavy)
  max_rounds: 4, retry: 1   (resume-heavy)

Compare accumulated total_cost_usd, NOT token counts: cache reads bill at a
fraction of input price and a raw token count flatters whichever side reads more
cache.
acceptance_criteria:
- Both configurations run over the same epic from the same starting commit.
- The two total_cost_usd figures, the round/attempt counts and the wall-clock
  times are recorded in this issue's notes.
- max_rounds and retry defaults in config are set from the result, and
  plans/headless.md is updated to state the measured outcome rather than the
  hypothesis.
notes:
bd-auto attempt 1/2 failed at stage "implement" on 2026-08-17T06:11:35Z:
worker session terminated by API session limit before reporting; no work product
MEASURED 2026-08-17. Harness: scripts/resume-vs-fresh.sh (make resume-vs-fresh), summariser scripts/resume_vs_fresh_report.py.

Method. Both arms drain the SAME fixture epic from the SAME starting commit (fixture base 1226a508), in their own throwaway git repo with its own beads database, differing in nothing but the two knobs. The fixture forces exactly one recovery per issue: a run: pipeline stage mints a random token on its first invocation for an issue and fails, printing the line the worker must add, so no worker can pass round one and every worker can pass round two. Both arms therefore spend the SAME six model processes on the same work; the only variable is whether process two continues the session or replaces it. Confirmed from the transcripts: the resume arm reuses one session id across rounds, the fresh arm starts a new one per attempt. Task per issue: read six files under docs/ and summarise them, so the fresh attempt pays a real re-derivation rather than a token one. Model sonnet, 3 issues, pipeline implement + verify (no reviewer, to keep the round count deterministic).

RESULT (3 issues, sonnet)
| arm    | config                | done | processes | attempts | total_cost_usd | wall clock |
| fresh  | max_rounds 1, retry 3 | 3/3  | 6         | 6        | $1.7210        | 264s       |
| resume | max_rounds 4, retry 1 | 3/3  | 6         | 3        | $1.4055        | 195s       |

Resume is 18.3% cheaper and 26% faster. It won on every issue, not on one outlier:
  fresh   fx-k8n.1 $0.6361 / fx-k8n.2 $0.5139 / fx-k8n.3 $0.5710   (2 attempts, 1 round each)
  resume  fx-k8n.1 $0.3888 / fx-k8n.2 $0.5103 / fx-k8n.3 $0.5065   (1 attempt, 2 rounds each)
Zero infra retries in either arm.

Rehearsal, independent data point: 1 issue on haiku gave $0.1061 resume against $0.1648 fresh, -35.6%, and 46s against 101s.

Tokens, for completeness only (cost is the comparison; cache reads bill far below input price):
  fresh   input 144   output 15956  cache read 2969221  cache creation 98412
  resume  input 100   output  8292  cache read 1982817  cache creation 114334

The plan's counterargument was that a resumed session re-sends its whole transcript each turn, so its input is strictly larger. True per turn, wrong in aggregate: the resume arm read fewer cached tokens and produced half the output. A fresh attempt does not only re-derive its plan, it re-runs the exploration, and every tool result that produces is then re-sent on every remaining turn of the new session.

DEFAULTS SET FROM THIS. max_rounds 3, retry 1 — unchanged in value, now measured rather than assumed, and with the roles fixed the way the plan wanted: rounds primary, retry the safety net. 3 rather than 2 because the dogfood run needed three to clear a hard review; not more, because nothing past round two was measured and a long attempt eventually loses its cache prefix to the 5-minute TTL and its transcript to an autocompact. retry 1 because a fresh attempt is the only escape from a session that has gone wrong in itself. Recorded in internal/config/config.go, internal/config/template.go, .beads-auto.yaml, plans/headless.md and README.md.

LIMITS, stated. The fixture's re-derivation is six small files; a repo with heavier exploration should widen the gap, one with almost none should narrow it. Both arms ran sonnet, not the default opus, so the ratio transfers and the dollars do not. Only one recovery round per issue was exercised. The reviewer was left out of the pipeline to keep round counts deterministic, so this measures the worker loop, which is what these two knobs govern.

TWO BUGS FOUND WHILE BUILDING IT, filed deferred:
  beads-auto-imp-so5 - beads' post-checkout hook imports .beads/issues.jsonl back over the database when the next attempt's worktree is created, deleting the failure note bd-auto had just written. A fresh attempt gets no feedback in its prompt at all, so notes are its whole feedback channel; without them the fresh arm burned all four attempts repeating one mistake. Reproduced with git alone. The harness disables beads' hooks in the fixture for exactly this reason, or the experiment would have measured the bug.
  beads-auto-imp-o4q - permissions: auto, the shipped default, refused a headless worker every file write; it looped 226s and $0.41 and died on the no-progress check. The fixture uses bypass.

title: Per-issue pipeline and bd-auto issue run --issue X
description:
One issue end to end, standalone and debuggable before any wave logic exists.
The unified recovery loop with one feedback channel:

  mark := worktree.Snapshot(wt)                    // branch tip + dirty set
  res  := runner.Run(...)
  infra-failed  -> backoff, re-run the same round  // no round, no attempt spent
  interrupted   -> return; attempt counter untouched
  !Changed      -> hard fail the attempt           // NOT another round
  !Terminal     -> feedback, next round
  guard fails   -> feedback, next round
  gate fails    -> feedback, next round
  review fails  -> feedback, next round

The progress check must come first and must be a hard failure. Every check below
it is satisfiable by stale state: after round 1 the issue is already closed, so
Terminal() passes on round 2 even if round 2 did nothing, and gitguard.Verify
passes on an unchanged branch. A no-op round would sail through to the reviewer,
which re-reads an identical diff, fails identically, and spends every remaining
round in an empty loop at full price.

Sessions persist to run state (Attempt.AgentID at state.go:38 becomes
WorkerSession and ReviewSession, written before the runner is invoked rather
than by a hook afterwards). Review notes go to .beads/auto/review/<id>.md.

The reviewer defaults to a FRESH session. Reviewer resume is available but off:
a resumed reviewer carries its own previous VERDICT: fail and is anchored to
checking whether its findings were addressed rather than re-judging the diff,
and it is the cheap half anyway since the diff dominates its input and must be
re-read after changes.
acceptance_criteria:
- bd-auto issue run --issue X drives one issue through implement, gate and review
  with resume rounds, using the fake runner in tests and claude for real.
- A gate failure, a review failure and a guard violation each produce a
  Resume: true request on the SAME session ID, with the worktree surviving.
- A round returning ok with no commit and no file change fails the attempt
  outright and does not consume the remaining rounds.
- fake returning infra-failed then ok re-runs the same round index, with neither
  the round nor the attempt counter advanced.
- A Caps().Resume == false variant reaches the same outcomes via fresh processes.
- discardAttempt fires only between attempts, never between rounds.

title: internal/worktree and internal/gitguard: own the worktree and close the git holes
description:
Worktree creation is currently Claude Code's job via `isolation: worktree` in the
agent frontmatter. Verified: `git worktree add` appears nowhere in the Go code,
only listWorktrees (merge.go:201) and `git worktree remove` (worker.go:174).
Deleting the plugin deletes worktree creation, so Go has to own the lifecycle.

internal/worktree:
- create at .beads/auto/wt/<issue> from the base SHA recorded at dispatch
- reuse on a later round and on a resumed run. The path must be stable, because
  `claude --resume` resolves a session against the project derived from cwd; a
  moved worktree is a lost session
- `git worktree prune` at drain start, plus adopt-or-recreate for the
  "worktree exists, branch does not" case
- removal only between attempts and after a successful merge

internal/gitguard replaces the PreToolUse deny at hook.go:280, whose
agent_id == "" guard (hook.go:348) silently stops firing headless.

Structural, at worktree creation. Two traps, both confirmed against this repo:
- --worktree and extensions.worktreeConfig are BOTH required; a plain git config
  inside a worktree writes the shared config and breaks the main checkout.
- core.hooksPath is ALREADY set here, to .beads/hooks, holding beads' pre-commit,
  pre-push, post-checkout, post-merge and prepare-commit-msg. Pointing it at a
  rejector dir disables every one of them inside worker worktrees, including the
  pre-commit that keeps issues.jsonl in sync. So the rejector dir is generated
  per run and CHAINS: reject if it is one bd-auto blocks, else exec the
  same-named hook under the previous hooksPath with "$@" (falling back to
  .git/hooks). Its own prepare-commit-msg appends a Bd-Auto: <issue>/<attempt>
  trailer before chaining.

What the structural half cannot catch: pre-merge-commit does not fire on a
fast-forward merge, and git rebase has no hook at all. pre-push does fire for
every push regardless of remote, so the push half is genuinely closed once
chaining works.

Post-hoc, against the base SHA recorded at dispatch:
- git merge-base --is-ancestor <base> <branch>
- git rev-list --min-parents=2 --count <base>..<branch> is 0
- EVERY commit in <base>..<branch> carries this run's Bd-Auto: trailer
- base branch SHA unchanged
- refs/remotes/origin/* unchanged

The trailer check is the one that closes the holes. After `git rebase
origin/main` the base is still an ancestor, there are still no merge commits,
and the local and remote refs are still unchanged, but base..branch now contains
origin's commits and those have no trailer. Same for a fast-forward merge.
acceptance_criteria:
- Worktrees created, reused, pruned and removed by Go; paths stable across rounds.
- Rejector hooks chain: a test asserts beads' own pre-commit still runs inside a
  worker worktree.
- Guard tests against temp repos with a fake origin: fast-forward merge from
  origin, rebase onto origin, push, and a clean branch. The first two must be
  caught by the trailer predicate, which the shape predicates alone do not catch.
- Rejection messages say what to do instead, not only what is forbidden.
close_reason: Closed

title: runner/claude and runner/fake adapters
description:
The only shipping backend, plus the scripted adapter that makes the whole engine
testable with zero model calls.

claude -p <task> --append-system-prompt <role> --model <m> --permission-mode auto
  --session-id <uuid> | --resume <uuid>
  --output-format stream-json --verbose --include-partial-messages
  --allowed-tools ...   (reviewer only)

All verified present in CLI 2.1.233. --include-partial-messages is what makes
the TUI activity line text-granular rather than tool-call-granular.

Two details that are easy to get wrong and expensive to debug:

- Cancellation must kill the process group. exec.CommandContext kills the direct
  child only, so a worker 40s into `go test ./...` leaves the test running and
  holding its worktree. Set SysProcAttr{Setpgid: true} and signal the group
  (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after a grace period).
- Usage is recorded as cost, not summed tokens. Across resume rounds the same
  prefix is billed repeatedly as cache reads at a fraction of input price, so
  summing input_tokens overstates a resumed attempt. Record total_cost_usd plus
  input/output/cache-read/cache-creation separately.

fake replays scripted results including Class, and records every Request it
receives so downstream tests can assert exactly what was asked for.
acceptance_criteria:
- Table tests on constructed argv for each role, resume and fresh.
- stream-json parsing yields tool-call and text events, plus the final result.
- Exit code / stderr map to Class; a usage-limit and a 429 both map to
  infra-failed.
- Cancelling the context kills a grandchild process, asserted in a test.
- Usage carries total_cost_usd and cache-read/cache-creation separately.
- fake records every Request and can script per-call Class sequences.

title: internal/runner: Runner interface, Class taxonomy and per-role config
description:
The seam everything else plugs into. Defines Runner, Request, Result,
Capabilities, Permissions, and the Class taxonomy the engine branches on before
anything else:

  ok | work-failed | infra-failed | interrupted

Class exists because "the process exited non-zero" is not one thing. Without it,
five parallel workers meeting one rate limit each burn three rounds and a fresh
attempt against a 429 and then park five good issues with a nonsense reason.
infra-failed must consume neither a round nor an attempt.

Also lands the runners: config block with per-role resolution over default, and
the two validation rules called out in the plan: a pipeline stage's agent: field
now names a key under runners: (a silent breaking change), and per-stage

- Runner, Request, Result (with Class and Err), Capabilities, Permissions defined.

title: bd-auto: headless engine with a swappable agent backend
description:
Invert bd-auto: Go owns control flow and spawns models as subprocesses, instead
of a live orchestrator context dispatching subagents through the Agent tool.

Today coordination is O(issues) in one append-only transcript that is re-sent
every turn, which is the context blow-up this project exists to fix. Model
invocation goes behind a Runner interface so the backend can be swapped without
touching the engine.

What bounds a run is a human-selected set of issues, chosen before any model is
spawned. There are no budgets, no per-request timeouts and no circuit breakers.

Full plan: plans/headless.md
acceptance_criteria:
- A drain launched from a Claude Code session via the rewritten skill grows the
  launching session by under 2k tokens regardless of epic size. This is the
  number every other issue here serves.
- A run never touches an issue the human did not select.
- go build ./... && go vet ./... && go test ./... passes at every child issue.

title: Plan: persistent graphify-backed codebase index initialised at each wave start
description:
We need a human plan/decision before implementing.

Idea: at the start of every bd-auto wave, initialise a persistent tool/service backed by graphify (the knowledge-graph skill) over the current codebase. Worker, reviewer and integrator agents then query that tool instead of grepping and reading files, so they can understand the codebase at a much lower token count.

Open questions for the human:
- Where does the graph live (graphify-out/ in the main checkout? shared read-only mount into each worktree?) and who owns its lifecycle?
- When is it built/refreshed — once per wave at dispatch, or incrementally after the integrator merges each wave?
- How do agents query it: a slash command / skill invocation, an MCP server, or a plain CLI the agents shell out to?
- Staleness policy: worktrees diverge from the base branch during a wave, so how do we signal that graph answers may lag the worker's own edits?
- Cost/benefit: graph build time and tokens vs. the per-agent context savings. Is it worth it below some issue count?
- Fallback: what agents do when the graph is missing, stale or the build fails.

Deliverable: a written plan (design doc or a set of child issues) that a bd-auto wave can then implement.
acceptance_criteria: A human has answered the open questions and either a design doc or a set of child implementation issues exists.
notes:
bd-auto attempt 1: delivered the design doc at plans/graph-index.md.

ask_user put the lifecycle question (build once per run / refresh per wave / consume only / measure first) to the human and was told nobody was watching, so no human answered any of the six open questions. The decisions in the doc are the worker's, and each is traceable to a measurement taken on this repo at a585bf5 rather than to an argument. The doc's 'What was assumed' section records this and names the two choices a human should push back on: that the index ships disabled until stage 4 measures it, and that tests are excluded from the corpus by default.

The measurements reframed the issue's premise. The build is free (AST-only, 0.92s, zero tokens), so the cost/threshold question is moot. But the index returns file:line and edges, never prose, so it replaces searching and not reading — the doc's staleness policy turns on that.

Acceptance criteria are met on the 'design doc' branch of the 'or'. Child implementation issues were not created: bd-auto files discovered work itself at the wave barrier, so the four proposed stages are tabled in the doc for a human to file.

title: Plugin packaging and required repo settings
description:
Package as a proper Claude Code plugin in this repo: .claude-plugin/plugin.json plus skills/, agents/, hooks/hooks.json, bin/. Load during development with claude --plugin-dir . and validate with claude plugin validate.

Repo settings this design REQUIRES, documented in the README and applied here:
- worktree.baseRef=head in settings, otherwise subagent worktrees branch from the default branch and a wave will not see the previous wave merge.
- .claude/worktrees/ added to .gitignore.
- .worktreeinclude if any gitignored file is needed inside worker worktrees. Note .beads/embeddeddolt must NOT be copied; bd already resolves the main repo database from inside a worktree.
- The session must run in an accepting permission mode. permissionMode in frontmatter is ignored for PLUGIN subagents, so five workers in a prompting mode would produce a prompt storm.
- Use ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} for every hook command path.
acceptance_criteria: claude plugin validate passes. A fresh clone plus claude --plugin-dir gives a working /bd-auto. Required settings are documented and applied.
close_reason: Plugin manifest, hooks.json, Makefile, gitignore and worktree.baseRef=head; claude plugin validate passes

title: Failure policy: retry once fresh, then park
description:
Uniform handling for a worker that errors, a gate that will not pass, or a review that fails twice.

First failure: discard the attempt (remove its worktree and branch), retry the issue with a FRESH worker seeded with the failure notes appended to the issue. Second failure: bd update --status=blocked --append-notes with the accumulated evidence, flag with bd human, and continue the run. A single bad issue must never stall the drain.

Retry count is configurable. Every attempt appends to the issue notes so the history is in beads rather than in a context window that is about to be compacted.
acceptance_criteria: An issue whose gate cannot pass ends the run blocked, flagged for human review, with both attempts notes on the issue, while the remaining issues in the epic still complete.
close_reason: Retry-once-fresh-then-park implemented in bd-auto worker fail; full lifecycle smoke-tested

title: Skill and slash command: the orchestrator protocol
description:
skills/bd-auto/SKILL.md defines what the main session does: validate the DAG, start the run, compute a wave, dispatch all workers for that wave IN A SINGLE MESSAGE so they run in parallel, collect capped reports, run the review stage (resuming the same worker with feedback on rejection, max 2 rounds), hit the wave barrier, invoke the integrator, then loop.

Keep it SHORT. It is re-injected by the SessionStart/PostCompact hooks, and a long skill defeats the purpose. Anything that can be enforced by the binary or a hook does not belong in prose here.

Entry point /bd-auto <epic-id> with flags for concurrency, autonomy mode and dry run. Dry run prints the wave plan and the resolved pipeline without dispatching.
acceptance_criteria: /bd-auto <epic> --dry-run prints the wave plan and pipeline. A real run dispatches a full wave in one message and reaches the wave barrier without the user intervening.
close_reason: skills/bd-auto/SKILL.md defines the orchestrator loop, kept short because the rehydration hook re-injects it

title: Wave integrator: dependency-ordered merge with conflict resolution
description:
At each wave barrier, merge the wave branches into main.

Order the bd-auto/<id> branches by the beads dependency graph, merge in that order, resolve conflicts, and require the gate to pass on the merged result. On resolution failure or gate failure, park the offending branch, reopen its issue with notes explaining the conflict, and flag it with bd human; the rest of the wave still lands.

Consider taking bd merge-slot around the merge so this stays correct if a second orchestrator ever runs concurrently. After a branch merges cleanly, remove its worktree (git worktree remove --force) so worktrees do not accumulate.

Note: worker worktrees are git-locked while their agent runs and released when it finishes, so cleanup must happen after the worker completes, not during.
acceptance_criteria: A wave of three branches, two clean and one conflicting, results in two merged issues and one parked-and-reopened issue with notes, gate green on main, and no leftover worktrees for the merged pair.
close_reason: bd-auto merge-order with Kahn topo sort + bd-integrator agent; ordering unit-tested, branch detection smoke-tested. Conflict resolution is agent behaviour, verified by eqc.13

title: Hooks: Stop autonomy driver and compaction rehydration
description:
The two hooks that make this survive long sessions.

Stop hook: armed ONLY while .beads/auto/run.json exists, so ordinary sessions in this repo are unaffected. While a run is active and the epic still has ready work, exit 2 with a precise next instruction on stderr (dispatch wave N: <ids>). This is the autonomy engine: the orchestrator physically cannot end the turn while claimable work remains. Honours the autonomy mode: auto drains the queue, wave pauses at each wave barrier, issue pauses after every issue.

SessionStart and PostCompact hooks: when a run is active, print the run state as context. This is the direct fix for the reported problem, the model forgetting its instructions after autocompact. The existing PreCompact bd prime hook stays.

Guard against a runaway loop: cap consecutive Stop-hook continuations and stop the run with a clear message if the wave number does not advance.
acceptance_criteria: With a run active the session cannot stop while ready work remains; with no run active the Stop hook is a no-op. After a forced /compact the session recovers the epic, wave and in-flight issues without the user restating anything.
close_reason: Stop autonomy driver + SessionStart/PostCompact rehydration; decision matrix unit-tested, hooks smoke-tested

title: Agent definitions: bd-worker, bd-reviewer, bd-integrator
description:
Three subagent definitions in agents/.

bd-worker (isolation: worktree): implements exactly one issue. Protocol: bd update <id> --claim, git switch -c bd-auto/<id>, read the issue with bd show including design/acceptance/notes, implement, run the gate, commit with -m referencing the issue ID, and report a CAPPED structured footer (issue, branch, status, <=5 line summary). It closes its issue only after gate and review pass. Discovered work is filed with bd create --deps discovered-from:<id> and deferred, never worked in the current run.

bd-reviewer: read-only tools. Reviews the worker diff against the issue acceptance criteria, returns a pass/fail verdict with specific actionable notes.

bd-integrator: runs in the main checkout, merges the wave branches in dependency order, resolves conflicts, and requires the gate to pass on the merged result.

Two hard constraints go in the worker prompt: worktree-isolated agents cannot use heredocs with unquoted delimiters or brace expansion (use git commit -m and the Write tool), and the report must stay within its size budget because it is the only thing that reaches the orchestrator context.

Consider omitting Agent from bd-worker tools so workers cannot recursively spawn their own subagents and multiply token cost.
acceptance_criteria: A worker dispatched against a single real issue claims it, works in its own worktree, commits to bd-auto/<id>, and returns a report within the size budget. Reviewer returns a structured verdict. Integrator merges two branches and runs the gate.
close_reason: bd-worker (isolation: worktree), bd-reviewer (read-only) and bd-integrator defined; worktree shell constraints and report cap encoded in the worker prompt. Live agent behaviour verified by eqc.13

title: Gate runner and pipeline stage executor
description:
Execute the configured per-issue pipeline. Stages are ordered and each is either agent: <subagent-name> or run: <shell command>. The built-in stages are implement (the worker itself) and gate (the configured build/test/lint commands); everything after is user-extensible, which is how a custom code-review pipeline plugs in.

The binary owns run: stages (execute, capture exit code, capture a bounded tail of output). agent: stages are executed by the orchestrator or worker via the Agent tool, so the binary only resolves and reports them. Stage output fed back into a retry must be truncated to a fixed budget so a failing test suite cannot blow the worker context.

Expose $BD_ISSUE, $BD_BRANCH and a path to the diff as environment to run: stages.
acceptance_criteria: A repo with a two-command gate and one custom run: stage executes all stages in order, stops at the first failure, and returns a structured result naming the failing stage with a bounded output tail.
close_reason: Gate runner and stage executor with bounded output; agent stages resolved not executed

title: Wave planner: bd-auto plan
description:
Compute the next wave of issues for a run.

Reads bd ready --parent <epic> --json, intersects with the run state (excluding parked, in-flight and already-done issues), caps at the configured concurrency (default 5), and emits the wave as JSON for the orchestrator to dispatch.

Prefer delegating dependency analysis to bd rather than reimplementing it: bd ready is already blocker-aware, and bd swarm validate already reports ready fronts and max parallelism. Call bd swarm validate at run start and surface its warnings (wrong dependency direction, orphans, cycles) rather than silently running on a bad DAG.
acceptance_criteria: Returns only issues with no unresolved blockers inside the epic; never returns a parked or in-flight issue; respects the concurrency cap; emits an empty wave when the epic is drained.
close_reason: bd-auto plan / plan --dispatch; delegates readiness to bd ready; smoke-tested incl. DAG exclusion

title: Go binary skeleton: config loader and run state
description:
Create bin/bd-auto, the single Go binary that backs both the hooks and the orchestrator helper commands.

Scope: cobra-style subcommand skeleton; parse .beads-auto.yaml (gate commands, ordered pipeline stages, concurrency, autonomy mode, retry count) with defaults for every field so a repo with no config still works; implement run start/status/stop over a state file at .beads/auto/run.json holding epic ID, wave number, dispatched issues, completed, parked, and a snapshot of the resolved config.

The run state file is the mechanism that makes a run survive autocompact, so treat its schema as the contract other issues code against. All output JSON on stdout, human text on stderr, so hooks can consume it.
acceptance_criteria: bd-auto run start --epic X writes valid run.json; run status emits JSON; run stop removes the armed flag; config loads with all defaults applied when .beads-auto.yaml is absent.
close_reason: Go binary, config loader and flock-guarded run state; unit tests incl. cross-process concurrency

title: bd-auto: beads-driven subagent orchestration plugin for Claude Code
description:
Claude Code plugin that drains a beads epic by dispatching one worktree-isolated subagent per issue, in dependency-ordered waves, with a configurable per-issue pipeline (gate, review, custom stages) and an end-of-wave integrator.

Problem: long multi-step sessions blow the context window, autocompact fires, and the model forgets its instructions even though every fact needed is already in the beads issues. Fix: each issue runs in a fresh, isolated subagent context; beads holds all durable state so the orchestrator can rehydrate after compaction; disjoint issues run in parallel.

Decisions locked (see design field): in-session subagents; worktree per worker; merge at end of wave; gate command + reviewer agent + user-extensible stages; retry once fresh then park; epic-scoped runs; concurrency 5; Go single binary; Stop hook armed only during a run.
design:
ARCHITECTURE
- bin/bd-auto: single Go binary. Both the hook entrypoint and the orchestrator helper. Subcommands: run start|status|stop, plan, gate, stage, hook <event>, merge-order.
- Run state at .beads/auto/run.json (epic, wave, dispatched, done, parked, config snapshot). This is what makes the run survive autocompact.
- Hooks (hooks/hooks.json): Stop (autonomy driver, exit 2 while work remains), SessionStart + PostCompact (rehydrate run state into context), SubagentStop (verify worker reached a terminal state), PreToolUse/Bash (bind agent_id to issue via the --claim call, block workers merging into main).
- Agents (agents/*.md): bd-worker (isolation: worktree), bd-reviewer (read-only), bd-integrator (main checkout, merges the wave).
- Skill (skills/bd-auto/SKILL.md): the orchestrator dispatch protocol, kept short and re-injected by hooks so compaction cannot erase it.
- Config .beads-auto.yaml at repo root: gate commands, ordered pipeline stages (each either agent: <name> or run: <cmd>), concurrency, autonomy mode, retry count.

RUN LIFECYCLE
1. bd swarm validate <epic> for DAG sanity, then bd-auto run start.
2. Wave = bd ready --parent <epic> ready-front, capped at concurrency (default 5).
3. Dispatch N bd-worker subagents in a single message so they run in parallel.
4. Worker: bd update <id> --claim, git switch -c bd-auto/<id>, implement, gate, commit, report a capped structured footer.
5. Review stage; on reject resume the SAME worker with feedback (retains context and worktree), max 2 rounds.
6. Worker closes its issue only after gate and review pass.
7. Wave barrier: bd-integrator merges bd-auto/* branches in dependency order into main, resolves conflicts, gate must pass on the merged result. Failures reopen the issue with notes and flag bd human.
8. Repeat until bd ready --parent <epic> is empty. The Stop hook enforces the loop.

VERIFIED FACTS
- bd resolves the main repo .beads/ from inside a git worktree (bd context reports "worktree: yes"), so workers use bd normally against the one shared DB. No redirect setup needed.
- bd ready --claim is atomic, so the wave is a race-safe pull queue rather than a push assignment.
- bd swarm validate already reports ready fronts, max parallelism and dependency-direction errors.
- Hooks fire inside subagents and carry agent_id + agent_type.
- Hooks cannot spawn agents (type: agent hooks only return ok/reason), so the Stop hook drives the loop and the main session does the dispatching.

CONSTRAINTS TO DESIGN AROUND
- Worktree-isolated agents cannot run shell constructs Claude Code cannot statically trace: no heredocs with unquoted delimiters, no brace expansion. Worker prompts must use git commit -m and the Write tool.
- permissionMode in frontmatter is ignored for plugin subagents, so the run needs the session already in an accepting permission mode or 5 workers cause a prompt storm.
- Subagent worktrees branch from the default branch, not parent HEAD. Set worktree.baseRef=head so each wave sees the previous wave merge.
- No git remote on this repo: all merging is local, and the CLAUDE.md push step does not apply.
close_reason: All 13 child issues completed and merged to main; plugin is built, packaged and dogfooded (eqc.13).

title: A non-judging role with no agent file still falls back to the reviewer's prompt
description:
internal/config/agents.go RolePrompt resolves a role with no agent file and no built-in of that name to the reviewer's prompt, on the reasoning that a custom stage judges a diff. That reasoning does not hold for every dispatched role any more: a hook (config.HookPoint, internal/drain/hooks.go) reads a finished report and nothing parses a verdict from it, so `agent: triager` with no triager.md is spawned with a system prompt telling it to review a diff and answer VERDICT: pass/fail about work it was not given.

beads-auto-imp-04l.5 made this visible rather than fixed it: hook roles are now in Config.PromptSources so `bd-auto config show` and the run's first log line report `origin: reviewer`, and the hook path deliberately parses no verdict, so the wrong prompt cannot fail anything. What it still costs is a call spent on a model working out that its instructions do not describe its task.

A fix would have to make the fallback depend on what the role is dispatched as rather than on nothing: PromptSource already carries Judging, so a non-judging role could fall back to a small generic prompt (or to no system prompt at all) instead of the reviewer's, and Config.Judging would need to stay the single place that answers the question. Worth deciding whether a role with no prompt should be an error at load instead, now that an agent file is the whole definition of one.

Found by the bd-auto worker on beads-auto-imp-04l.5, and filed at the wave barrier — deferred, so it waits for a human rather than being offered to the next run.

title: `bd-auto plan --dispatch` clears a live run's unmerged list, and now that list decides what may start
description:
internal/cmds/plan.go:71 calls wave.Record unconditionally, and wave.Record sets s.WaveIssues = nil before recording its own. There is no check that a drain is running, so `bd-auto plan --dispatch` in another terminal during a live run wipes that list.

It was already destructive under waves — the barrier merges WaveIssues, so clearing it made the barrier merge nothing. Continuous scheduling gives the same list a second job: wave.Joinable reads it to decide which ready issue would be implemented against a tree its dependency's branch is not in yet (see internal/wave/plan.go). Cleared mid-run, the scheduler stops holding dependents back and dispatches one against the wrong base, which is silent — the worker builds on a tree missing its dependency's work and nothing refuses it.

A fix is the check runstate.Active already provides and scripts/smoke.sh already makes (README, 'Scripts must not assume there is no run'): refuse --dispatch while a run is active, and say why. `bd-auto plan` without --dispatch reads nothing it would damage and should stay allowed.

Found by the bd-auto worker on beads-auto-imp-04l.2, and filed at the wave barrier — deferred, so it waits for a human rather than being offered to the next run.

title: The summary line is never clipped, so a narrow terminal cuts off the run total
description:
internal/tui/model.go View() writes m.summary() straight out, while the heading and the status line beside it both go through clip(). At 64 columns the summary is longer than the terminal and the terminal truncates it — and it truncates from the right, which is exactly where the two numbers the line exists for are. docs/screenshots/tui/tui-28-narrow.ansi shows it: the line ends at '... · barrier $0.0210 · run', with the run's elapsed time and the run's total cost both off the screen.

This predates the run clock: the barrier figure alone already pushed the line to 78 cells. The clock adds seven more.

A fix cannot just wrap clip() around it, because that ellipses in the same place and loses the same two numbers. It has to decide what gives way when the width runs out — the per-state counts are the obvious candidate, since a row-by-row reader can count them off the table above and the totals appear nowhere else.

Found by the bd-auto worker on beads-auto-imp-04l.6, and filed at the wave barrier — deferred, so it waits for a human rather than being offered to the next run.

title: Show the round in the STATE column, and the attempt in a column of its own
description:
## What is wanted

The state cell names the process — `worker`, `gate`, `reviewer` — but not which time round it is. A row that has been on `worker` for four minutes reads the same whether the worker is writing the code for the first time or fixing what the reviewer sent back twice. Two numbers say which: the feedback round, in the state cell, and the attempt, in a new column to the left of STATE.

    ISSUE                  WAVE ATT STATE          TIME     COST  ACTIVITY
    t-2                    2    1   reviewer (0)     25s  $0.4210  Read internal/store/store.go
    t-3                    2    2   worker (1)       23s        -  Bash
    t-4                    2    1   gate (1)       1m04s  $0.6602  the gate stage is running

They are different numbers and both are wanted: a round is another turn inside one worktree and one session, an attempt is that worktree and session thrown away and started again. `worker (1)` on attempt 2 is a run that has now spent two sessions on one issue, and until both are on screen that is invisible.

## Neither number leaves the engine today

This is the actual work. `Event` (internal/drain/bus.go:130) carries neither. The engine has all three counters and none reaches a watcher:

- the attempt-level `round` loop counter (internal/drain/issue.go:224),
- `stageRounds[stage]` (issue.go:214), the per-stage count that `stageBudget` bounds, and
- `t.Attempt`, the retry attempt.

All of them are written to run state by `recordRound` (internal/drain/drain.go:678), which is a file, not the stream the renderers read. So this needs `Round` and `Attempt` fields on `Event`, set wherever the state cell's value comes from — EventStageStart and EventIssueStart at least. `Event` is also the `--json` stream, so this is an additive change to that contract and should be documented as one.

## Which round counter

Per stage, zero-based, which is what the example asks for: `worker (0)`, `reviewer (0)`, `worker (1)`, `reviewer (1)`. `stageRounds` is already exactly this, and it is the number `max_rounds` bounds — so a reader watching `reviewer (2)` under `max_rounds: 3` can see the budget running out, which the attempt-level counter would not show. The attempt-level counter would also make the reviewer's number jump rather than count, since only worker turns increment it.

## The columns

Both additions are paid for by ACTIVITY, and together they are not cheap.

`colState` is 11, and internal/tui/model.go:915 documents why: "integrator" is 10, and the width was chosen against exactly that, deliberately rather than by accident. ` (0)` needs four more. The attempt column needs its own width on top.

Recommend a **3-wide column headed `ATT`**, between WAVE and STATE, rather than a 7-wide `ATTEMPT`. It is the only abbreviated header in a table of full words, and that is the lesser cost: ACTIVITY is about 21 cells on an 80-column terminal, and `ATTEMPT` plus the round would take more than half of what is left. The value is one digit in every run anyone will watch. Judge it with `make tui-shots` at 80 columns before settling.

Update the comment at internal/tui/model.go:915 with whatever is chosen — it explains a set of widths, and a stale explanation of widths that moved is exactly the drift the repo's conventions warn about.

## The rest

- A terminal row keeps its own word (done, parked, failed, killed) and shows no round: no process is running to count. The attempt it ended on still means something and should stay.
- Consider the plain renderer's stage lines too, once the fields exist. One vocabulary across the renderers is the point of the bus.
- Screenshot harness and README's watching-a-run example both show this table and both change.
acceptance_criteria:
- The STATE cell shows the round for a running stage, zero-based and per stage, and nothing for a terminal row.
- A column to the left of STATE shows the attempt.
- Round and attempt are carried on the event stream, not read from run state by the view.
- The state column still holds "integrator" without clipping, and ISSUE and WAVE do not move.
- The table is still readable at 80 columns, with ACTIVITY showing something useful.
- The comment at internal/tui/model.go:915 matches the widths it describes.

title: Show how long the run has been going in the wave table
description:
## What is missing

Every clock in the TUI is per issue. A row shows how long *that* issue has been in flight (`Row.Elapsed`, internal/tui/model.go:171), and the summary line shows money for the whole run — `run total $1.8947` — but no time for it. So the one number a person watching a drain asks first, how long has this been going, is the one number not on screen.

## Where it goes

The summary line, beside the total it already carries (`m.summary()`, internal/tui/model.go:1257), so the run's two totals sit together:

    3 running · 1 done · 0 parked · 0 killed · run total 12m04s $1.8947

The heading is the other candidate (`m.heading()`, :1179) but it is already carrying the epic, the wave and the scope size, and it is the line that gets clipped first on a narrow terminal.

## Where the clock starts

Start it at `EventRunStart`. The Model has no run-level start time today — rows carry their own — so this is a new field set from the event's `At`, which is also what makes the live number agree with `DrainReport.Seconds` in the final report. Two numbers on the same screen that disagree about how long a run took would be worse than the missing one.

`runstate.State.StartedAt` (internal/runstate/state.go:58) is the other possible origin and is deliberately not it: it survives a resume, so a run picked up the next morning would show a clock including the hours nobody was running anything.

Freeze it when the run ends, the way a finished row freezes at `Ended`. The last thing the table says should be how long it took, not a number still climbing after the run is over.

## The rest of it

- `duration()` already formats these (used by the row clocks), so the shape matches — `2m43s`, not seconds.
- The transcript view and the barrier view read the same model; decide whether they show it too, or whether it stays on the table.
- The screenshot harness (`make tui-shots`, BD_AUTO_SHOTS) photographs the table in every state, so the shots change. The clock must come from `m.now()`, which is already injectable, or every shot becomes nondeterministic.
- README's watching-a-run example block shows the summary line and needs the new field.

- The wave table shows the run's elapsed time, formatted like the row clocks, beside the run total cost.
- The clock starts at the run-start event and agrees with the seconds in the final run report.
- It stops when the run ends and shows the final duration.
- Screenshot tests are deterministic and updated; make check passes.

title: Somewhere to hang an agent that reads a result: post-verdict, post-barrier and end-of-run hooks
description:
## What was asked for

A custom post-result interpreter: an agent of the repo's own that reads what a stage or a run produced and does something with it. Today there is nowhere to put one.

## What interprets a result today

Worth listing, because most of it is deliberately not a model and should stay that way:

- **reviewer** — the only model that judges an issue's output. A role, with a prompt, in the pipeline.
- **integrator** — the only other model the engine spawns, and only for a merge conflict (internal/drain/integrate.go:549, prompt in text.go:128).
- **feedback composition** — every string sent back to a worker after a failed gate or review is Go, in internal/drain/text.go, and its doc comment argues it is one voice on purpose.
- **gate blame** — which merge turned the wave gate red is worked out by peeling and re-merging (integrate.go:794), not by asking anything.
- **discovery triage** — `internal/drain/triage.go` stages what workers found; deduplication is rarity-weighted text matching in `internal/similar`, with no model anywhere. A human runs `bd-auto triage` to turn a finding into an issue, fold it into one, or discard it.
- **handoff** — the pull request body is assembled in Go (handoff.go).

So the pipeline is per-issue and stops at the verdict. There is no point after the verdict, after the barrier, or at the end of a run where a repo can attach anything, model or script.

## The shape to consider

Named hooks, each taking the same two forms a pipeline stage already takes — `agent: <role>` or `run: <command>`:

- `on_issue_end` — the issue's verdict and its Report.
- `on_barrier` — the IntegrateReport: what merged, what conflicted, what the gate said.
- `on_run_end` — the DrainReport, before or beside the handoff.

The inputs already exist as JSON types with stable field names, so a hook gets a path to the report the way a `run:` stage gets $BD_DIFF_FILE, and an `agent:` hook gets the same path named in its task text.

## The question that has to be answered first

**What authority does a hook have?** An interpreter that can only write — notes, a summary, a filed finding — is a different thing from one that can park an issue, fail a run or block a handoff. Start advisory: a hook reads, and its output is recorded and shown, and it cannot change a verdict. Give it authority later, explicitly, per hook, if something needs it. Getting this backwards puts an unreviewed prompt in the path of every verdict the engine reaches.

The other constraints are the engine's existing ones and are not negotiable: one writer per issue, so a hook must not write to an issue whose worker is live; a hook is not a place to run git; and a hook that hangs must not hang the run, so it needs the same timeout treatment a `run:` stage gets.

## The obvious first customer

Triage. Deciding whether a discovered finding is new work, a duplicate of something already filed, or noise is exactly a post-result interpretation, it is currently `internal/similar` plus a human, and the repo has measured evidence about what workers discover (2.27 issues created per issue closed, nine parents with exactly two children each — the constant-two pattern that made triage the default). An `on_barrier` agent with the triage staging file as its input is a real use for this rather than a hypothetical one, and it is a good test of whether advisory-only is enough.

## Notes

Design first. This issue is worth a decision — the hook points, the input contract, and the authority rule — before any of it is built. It also depends on agents being definable at all (beads-auto-imp-04l.4): a hook that names an agent is not much use while every custom agent silently gets the reviewer's prompt.
design: Advisory before authoritative. An interpreter whose output is recorded and shown is useful immediately and cannot make the engine wrong; one that can park an issue or fail a run puts an unreviewed repo-authored prompt in the path of every verdict, which is a much larger promise to make in the same change.
acceptance_criteria:
- A written decision covering: which hook points exist, what each receives, whether output is advisory or authoritative, and what a hook may not do.
- Hooks take agent: or run:, the same two forms a pipeline stage takes, and are validated at config load like one.
- A hook's input is a file of already-defined report JSON, not a new serialisation invented for the hook.
- A hook cannot hang a run, and cannot write to an issue whose worker is live.
- Hook output reaches the run report and the renderers.
- Documented in README and the config comments with a worked example.
- make check passes.
close_reason: Closed

title: An agent is one file: .beads-auto/agents/<name>.md, frontmatter plus prompt, spliceable and materialised by bd init
description:
## Where this stands today

Half an agent is already definable and the half that is missing is the half that matters.

**Definable now:** any key under `runners:` is a role — provider, model, permissions, allowed_tools, denied_tools, extra_args, timeout, resume, each resolved over `default` (internal/config/runners.go:96). `pipeline: agent: <role>` validates against those roles at config load (config.go:483), so wiring a role into the pipeline works and a typo fails before anything spawns.

**Not definable now:** the prompt. `prompts.For` knows exactly three names (prompts/prompts.go), and `Engine.promptFor` (internal/drain/drain.go:424) falls back to the **reviewer prompt** for anything else — silently, on the reasoning that a custom stage is a judging stage. So `agent: security` today is the shipped reviewer wearing a different model and tool list, and nothing on screen says so. That is the whole of the gap.

There is already a seam to hang the fix on: `Engine.Prompt func(role runner.Role) (string, error)` (drain.go:225) is the injection point, so a file-backed resolver needs no surgery in the engine.

## The shape

One file per agent, in `.beads-auto/agents/<name>.md`, frontmatter for the runner spec and the body for the system prompt:

    ---
    model: sonnet
    permissions: scoped
    allowed_tools: [Read, Grep, "Bash(git diff:*)"]
    ---
    You judge a diff for security defects only.

    {{BUILTIN}}

An agent is then a standalone thing you can read, diff and copy between repos, rather than a yaml key in one file and a prompt somewhere else.

### Splices

`{{GRAPH}}` already exists in spirit: `prompts.Graph` substitutes the index path into a section appended to whichever role prompt was resolved, and only when an index exists (prompts/prompts.go, internal/drain/graph_attach.go). Custom prompts must keep getting that treatment, and the splices become a documented surface rather than an internal detail:

- `{{BUILTIN}}` — the shipped prompt for a role of this name, so a repo can add to the reviewer instead of replacing it. Empty for a name with no built-in, which is not an error.
- `{{GRAPH}}` — the code-index section, empty when there is no index. Today it is appended; letting a file place it is the same substitution with a chosen position.
- `{{VERDICT}}` — see below.

Document them in the config comments, in README, and in the materialised files themselves.

### The verdict contract is the sharp edge

`ParseVerdict` (internal/drain/issue.go:736) requires a judging stage's final message to start with `VERDICT: PASS` or `VERDICT: FAIL`, and no verdict line fails closed — silence is a fail. A hand-written judging prompt that does not say so fails every issue it ever sees, and the failure looks like a strict reviewer rather than a broken prompt. So bd-auto appends the contract to any judging stage's prompt itself, and `{{VERDICT}}` only chooses where it lands. Do not leave it to the author to remember.

### Resolution and precedence

- A role's prompt resolves: `.beads-auto/agents/<role>.md` if present, else the built-in for that name, else the current reviewer fallback.
- The fallback stops being silent. `bd-auto config show` reports, per role, where its prompt came from — a file path, "builtin", or "reviewer (no prompt of its own)" — and the run log says the same once at start. A repo must be able to tell a configured agent from an accidental one.
- yaml `runners:` overrides frontmatter. The yaml is the run's configuration surface and is where `default` resolution already lives; the file carries the agent's own defaults.

### Read it in the main checkout, never in a worktree

prompts/ is `go:embed`ed for a stated reason: a run spawns processes in worktrees, and the prompts do not live there. Reading agent files from disk reintroduces exactly that problem — a worktree may be on a commit where the file differs or does not exist. Resolve every prompt once, in the main checkout, at config load, and carry the text in the request. A missing or unreadable file named by a pipeline in use is a config-load error, in keeping with the rest of this config.

## bd init materialises the built-ins

`bd-auto init` writes worker.md, reviewer.md and integrator.md into `.beads-auto/agents/` verbatim, as though the user had written them. A repo's behaviour is then traceable in its own git history, and a bd-auto upgrade that rewrites a shipped prompt cannot silently change how that repo's runs behave.

The cost is the other half of the same coin and has to be handled, not just noted: a materialised file pins the prompt, so an improved shipped prompt never reaches that repo. Therefore:

- Frontmatter records provenance — that it came from the built-in, and which bd-auto version wrote it.
- There is a way to see that the shipped prompt has moved on since: a diff against the built-in, and an explicit update. `bd-auto agents` is the natural home (list what each role resolves to, diff one against its built-in, re-materialise on request).
- A repo that would rather track upstream writes a short file containing `{{BUILTIN}}` plus its own additions, and the documentation says so next to the materialised files.
- init never clobbers: same discipline as config.Write and ErrConfigExists, with --force to replace.

## Notes

Once this exists, `agent:` on the implement stage (beads-auto-imp-04l.3) means a repo can supply its own implementer as well as its own reviewer, which is the ask behind both issues.
design: One file per agent rather than yaml wiring plus a separate prompt file: an agent becomes a standalone entity that can be read and copied whole, which is also the shape Claude Code uses for .claude/agents, so it is already familiar. yaml keeps the last word so a repo can override a shared agent file without editing it.
acceptance_criteria:
- A file at .beads-auto/agents/<name>.md defines a usable agent: its body is the system prompt and its frontmatter sets the same fields runners: sets.
- Dropping in reviewer.md overrides the shipped reviewer with no other config change.
- {{BUILTIN}}, {{GRAPH}} and {{VERDICT}} substitute as documented, and a splice with nothing to splice yields nothing rather than an error or a literal.
- A judging stage always carries the VERDICT contract whether or not the author wrote one.
- Every prompt is read in the main checkout; no model process reads an agent file from a worktree.
- A pipeline naming an agent whose file is missing or unparseable fails at config load, naming the path.
- bd-auto config show reports the resolved prompt source for every role in the pipeline.
- bd-auto init writes the three built-in agents into .beads-auto/agents/ with provenance in their frontmatter, and refuses to overwrite without --force.
- There is a documented way to see that a materialised agent has drifted from the shipped prompt, and to take the new one.
- README and the .beads-auto.yaml comments document the directory, the frontmatter fields, the splices and the precedence rule.
- make check passes; tests cover resolution order, precedence, a missing file, and each splice.
notes: Materialising the built-ins at init is a deliberate trade: traceability of what a repo actually ran, paid for with prompts that no longer follow the binary. The provenance frontmatter and the drift check are what make that trade honest rather than a trap.
close_reason: An agent is one file: .beads-auto/agents/<role>.md, frontmatter over the prompt. Resolution file>builtin>reviewer, reported by config show, bd-auto agents and the run log; splices BUILTIN/GRAPH/VERDICT; init materialises the built-ins with provenance and agents diff/update handle the drift.

title: Every pipeline stage names its agent, and the built-in stages stop being magic
description:
## The confusion

In .beads-auto.yaml the pipeline reads:

    pipeline:
      - stage: implement
      - stage: gate
      - stage: review
        agent: reviewer

Two of those three steps say nothing about who runs them, and the one that does uses a different vocabulary from the step itself. Nothing on the page connects `implement` to the `worker` role under `runners:`, and nothing says why `gate` has no agent while `review` does.

## The rule to make true

A stage is a step. `agent:` says who runs it. `run:` says it is a shell command. Neither means it is a built-in deterministic stage. Written out:

    pipeline:
      - stage: implement
        agent: worker        # was implicit and unoverridable
      - stage: gate          # no agent - deterministic gate commands
      - stage: review
        agent: reviewer
        max_rounds: 3

## What is in the way

`Stage.Kind()` (internal/config/config.go:159) matches on the stage *name* first, so `stage: implement` returns "builtin-implement" whatever `agent:` says — the field is silently ignored rather than rejected, which is the worst of the three options. `Load` also injects `{Stage: StageImplement}` at the head of any pipeline that omits it (config.go:398). The role the implement stage runs is hardcoded downstream.

## Scope

- Honour `agent:` on the implement stage, so a repo can put its own role there. This is the same change that makes a custom implementer possible, which is why it comes before beads-auto-imp-04l.4 rather than after.
- `gate` stays the one agentless built-in, and the config comment says why: it is commands, not judgement.
- A pipeline that still says `- stage: implement` with no agent keeps meaning `worker`. No existing config changes behaviour.
- The generated template (internal/config/template.go) writes the agent out explicitly, because the template is where most people learn the schema.
- README's pipeline section and .beads-auto.yaml's comment block state the rule in one sentence.

## The one thing that is not just naming

The implement stage is special beyond its name: it is where the worktree, the branch and the session that later stages resume against are created. Making its role configurable must not turn that lifecycle into something any stage can claim. Decide explicitly whether "the first stage owns the worktree" or "the implement stage owns the worktree" is the invariant, and write it down where issue.go can be read against it.
design: Chosen over renaming the worker role to implementer, and over renaming stages to role names. Keeping stage names as steps and role names as agents costs no churn in run.json, the TUI, README or prompts/, and the homogeneity comes from every stage answering the same question — who runs this — rather than from the two vocabularies being forced into one.
acceptance_criteria:
- agent: on the implement stage selects the role that runs it, and a name that is not a defined role fails at config load with the same message the review stage already gives.
- A config that omits agent: on implement behaves exactly as before.
- The generated template names an agent on every stage that has one, and no agent on gate.
- README and the config comments state the stage/agent rule once, in one place each.
- make check passes.

title: Infra backoff is useless against a plan limit: parse the reset time the CLI already tells us
description:
Infra backoff retries 5 times at 5s doubling, roughly 75 seconds total. A session or plan limit resets in tens of minutes: drain 6 hit "You have hit your session limit · resets 3:20pm (Europe/Berlin)" at 12:38, a 26 minute wait. Every retry was spent against a wall that had no chance of moving.

The CLI states the reset time in the result text and bd-auto discards it. At minimum parse it into the stop reason so a human knows when re-running is worth anything. Better: when the reset is known and near, wait for it rather than burning attempts; when it is far, stop the run and say so in one legible line.

- A recognised reset time appears in the run stop reason and in the parked notes.
- Backoff does not exhaust retries against an outage whose reset is known to be beyond the retry window.

title: The wave table renders every row whatever the terminal height is, so a long run scrolls its own summary off the screen
description:
internal/tui/model.go View() writes the heading, one line per issue in m.order, every barrier row, the summary, the status line and the key line, and never consults m.height(). Only the transcript view windows itself (internal/tui/detail.go bodyHeight/window). A 30-issue scope on a 20-row terminal renders 36 lines: the terminal keeps the last 20, so the heading and the first rows are gone, and there is no key to scroll them back. Adding the barrier block makes this easier to hit — a wave's barrier adds a row per branch plus a gate row plus a rule.

A fix has to window the table the way the transcript is windowed: a body height, an offset the cursor keeps in view, and something on screen saying how many rows are off it in each direction. The summary, status and key lines are the fixed chrome and must survive; they are what says whether the run is still moving.

title: `bd-auto issue run` sees none of the event stream, so its gate is as silent as the table's used to be
description:
internal/cmds/issue.go:72 builds the engine with a Sink and no Bus, so the run-level events never reach it: it renders raw runner events through progressSink (issue.go:112) and nothing else. That means the stage boundaries added for beads-auto-imp-j5a.6 are invisible there, and so is everything else on the bus.

The effect is the one that issue fixed for the wave table: during the gate, and during any `run:` stage, `bd-auto issue run` prints nothing at all and looks hung, for however long `go test ./...` takes. Its own doc comment calls it 'the thing to reach for when something is wrong', which is exactly when a silent stretch is most expensive.

A fix would give issueRun a Bus with drain.PlainRenderer(os.Stderr) attached, alongside or instead of progressSink — the two overlap, since PlainRenderer already renders activity events with their role — and would need to settle which of them owns stderr so a reader does not get every tool call twice.

title: TestConcurrentQuestionsQueueIndependently is flaky: the queue is ordered by enqueue, not by AskedAt
description:
internal/ask/ask_test.go:225 asserts Pending()[0].AskedAt is not after Pending()[1].AskedAt, but the two orderings are set at different moments and can disagree. Broker.Ask stamps q.AskedAt = b.now() at internal/ask/ask.go:371, before it takes any lock; Broker.enqueue (ask.go:449) appends to b.order under b.mu, and Pending (ask.go:475) returns questions in b.order. Two goroutines asking at once can stamp in one order and reach the lock in the other, so Pending comes back with the later timestamp first. Reproduces on the unmodified tree at roughly 1 run in 8 under `go test -race -count=1 -run TestConcurrentQuestionsQueueIndependently ./internal/ask/`. A fix has to pick which ordering is the contract — Pending's doc comment says oldest first — and make the other follow it: either stamp AskedAt inside enqueue under the lock, or sort Pending by AskedAt as ask.go:689 already does elsewhere.

title: Refresh the code index at the wave barrier, and measure whether it paid for itself
description:
Stage 4 of plans/graph-index.md, and the stage that decides whether the index feature stays.

Run `graphify update` at each wave barrier after the integrator merges, so wave N+1 navigates wave N's codebase rather than the run's base commit. The refresh costs under a second and no tokens, so there is no cost argument for accepting the staleness.

Then measure. Following scripts/resume-vs-fresh.sh, drain one fixture epic twice from the same commit, with the index enabled and disabled, and compare total_cost_usd — never summed tokens, since cache reads bill at a fraction of input price and would flatter whichever arm reads more transcript.

The measurement matters because planning showed the saving is narrower than the original idea assumed: `graphify query` returns a truncated list of file:line and never prose, so the index can replace an agent's search phase but not its reading. The cheap exact tools (god_nodes at ~60 tokens, get_node at ~100) are where any real win should show up. Flip `graph.enabled` to true by default only if the number supports it; this repo sets knobs from measurements, as the max_rounds comment in .beads-auto.yaml records.

Depends on the index existing, so it cannot start until stages 1-3 land.

title: Build the graphify code index and offer it to the roles as a tool server
description:
Stages 1-3 of plans/graph-index.md, which beads-auto-imp-tv9 planned but deliberately did not implement.

Add an internal/graph package that writes a generated .graphifyignore and runs `graphify extract --code-only --out .beads/auto/graph` in the main checkout, stamping the commit it was built from. Attach the resulting graph to worker, reviewer and integrator runs via a new attachGraph that mirrors attachAsk in internal/drain/ask.go, and add the prompt sections telling each role that the index is a finding aid whose every fact must be confirmed by reading the file.

Three things were verified against graphify 0.9.30 during planning and each will break a naive implementation. `graphify.serve` imports `mcp`, which a plain `graphify` install does not pull in, so the preflight must confirm the `graphifyy[mcp]` extra rather than merely that graphify is on PATH. `graphify extract` writes no `graphify-out/.graphify_python` (only the skill's build path does), so the interpreter must be resolved from the `graphify` binary's shebang — guessing `python3` fails under `uv tool install`. And the MCP server offers ten tools, three of which (`list_prs`, `get_pr_impact`, `triage_prs`) reach GitHub; ToolServer.Tools must name only the seven graph tools, or a worker running behind the no-push git guard gets a route straight through it.

Ships with `graph.enabled: false`. Everything fails open: no graphify, no extra, or a failed build means no tool, no prompt text, and a run that behaves exactly as it does today.
