title: Show the barrier in the table: a merge is work, and right now it is one status line and a frozen screen
description:
A wave barrier merges every branch, spawns a model for any conflict, runs the gate on the merged result, rolls back and blames a branch when the gate goes red, reconciles bd and files the wave's discoveries. It can take minutes and it spends real money. The table shows one line of it:

    wave 2 integrating: merging 3 branches

and then nothing changes until it is over, when that line is replaced by 'wave 2 integrated: 2 merged, 1 parked, gate failed'. Every row above it is frozen on its final state. There is no way to tell a barrier that is resolving a conflict from one that has hung.

Three separate reasons the screen is empty, all of them fixable:

1. The barrier's model never reaches the bus at all. Workers get a tagged sink from forIssue (internal/drain/drain_wave.go:472), but the barrier runs on the top-level engine, and internal/cmds/drain.go:118 builds that engine with no Sink. The conflict resolver — the one model invocation integration ever makes (internal/drain/integrate.go:507) — streams into nothing.

2. There are only two barrier events, and they are the two ends. EventWaveIntegrating (integrate.go:198) carries every branch at once, EventWaveEnd (drain_wave.go:544) carries the whole result at once, and between them is however long it takes. Nothing marks one branch starting, one branch landing, the gate running, or the rollback that follows a red gate.

3. The TUI already receives more than it shows. integrated() (internal/tui/model.go:650) folds exactly two facts out of IntegrateReport back into the rows — a parked merge and a resolved one — and drops the rest: per-branch outcome (clean, resolved, parked, skipped), the conflicted paths, per-merge Usage and Seconds, the gate's results, which branch a red gate was blamed on, what was reconciled, what was filed. The barrier's own cost is accumulated into m.barrier (model.go:179) and folded into the run total, so it is spent but never shown as a line anyone can look at.
design:
Give the barrier its own block in the table, laid out in the same columns as the wave above it, so it reads without learning a second display. Something along the lines of:

    ISSUE                 WAVE  STATE     TIME     COST    ACTIVITY
    > kv-ctf.2            2     merged      3s        -    clean, no conflicts
      kv-ctf.4            2     resolving  47s  $0.0210    Edit(internal/wave/plan.go)
      kv-ctf.7            2     parked      1s        -    git would not merge: ...
      gate                2     running    12s        -    go test ./...

A row per branch, the same states-and-activity vocabulary the wave rows use, and a gate row that says what is running rather than leaving the screen still. Barrier cost belongs on its own line in the summary, not only inside the run total.

What it needs underneath:

- A sink for the barrier. e.Bus.Sink(wave, issue) already tags by issue and the conflict is always for a specific branch, so tag the integrator's events to that issue — the same choice integrate.go:514 already makes for the transcript path. Then the row for the branch being resolved shows the integrator's live tool calls, exactly as it showed the worker's.
- Per-branch and per-stage events: merge-start, merge-end with the outcome, gate-start, gate-end. Note the contract in internal/drain/bus.go — every kind is handled by every renderer — so the plain and JSON renderers move with the TUI.
- Per-merge Usage and Seconds are already on drain.Merge (integrate.go:53-63), so the cost and time columns need no new plumbing once the events carry them.
- A red gate is the interesting case and the one worth rendering well: the gate peels branches back one at a time until it goes green, and parks the one it lands on. The block should show that happening — rolling back, and which branch ended up blamed — rather than only the verdict.

Ordered after beads-auto-imp-j5a.1: this adds rows to the same table and wants the same things, and a barrier row is exactly where 'enter opens the transcript' pays off twice, since the integrator writes one at LogPath(issue, attempt, 0, integrator).
acceptance_criteria: A barrier renders as a labelled block with one row per branch, each carrying state, elapsed time, cost and activity, plus a gate row. A conflict being resolved shows the integrator's live tool calls against that branch's row, so a resolving barrier is visibly distinguishable from a hung one. A red gate shows the rollback and names the branch it blamed. The barrier's own cost appears as its own figure and still agrees with the run total. Clean merges, resolved merges, parked merges and skipped branches are each visible as what they are. The plain and JSON renderers handle every new event kind. Tests feed a synthetic barrier through the model and assert on View(); a screenshot scene covers a barrier mid-resolution and one with a red gate.
close_reason: Closed

title: The table says 'running' where it could say which role is running: worker, reviewer, gate, integrator
description:
An issue's row says 'running' for its whole life. It says nothing about which of the several processes an issue takes is running right now — the worker, a reviewer, the gate, the integrator, or a custom stage the repo configured.

The information is already on the wire. internal/drain/bus.go:186 tags every activity event with the role that produced it (re.Role), and internal/tui/model.go never reads e.Role at all: apply() folds EventActivity into the row's text and usage and drops the role on the floor. The single-issue plain renderer already prints it — internal/cmds/issue.go:119-128 writes '[worker]', '[reviewer]' in front of every line — so the TUI is the one view that hides it.

Roles are not a fixed list. runner.BuiltinRoles() is worker, reviewer and integrator, but an agent stage runs under whatever role the config names for it (internal/drain/issue.go:401, role = Cfg.Role(s.Agent)), so the column has to render an arbitrary configured name.

There is a second half that the event stream cannot answer, and it is the more misleading one. Non-model stages emit nothing: the built-in gate and any 'run' command stage execute without a runner, and grep confirms the only per-issue events during an attempt come from the runner's own sink (internal/drain/drain.go:450). So while the gate is running the row keeps showing the worker's last tool call with the clock still climbing — it looks like a worker that has stalled, which is precisely the reading the display exists to prevent. The same gap sits between rounds and between stages.
design:
Two parts, and the first is nearly free.

1. Record the role on the Row as activity arrives, and render it where the row currently says 'running'. Terminal states keep their own words — done, parked, failed, killed, stopped are outcomes and no role applies. The 'killing' and 'asking' overrides at internal/tui/model.go:955-963 must still win over the role: a worker waiting on a human is more urgent than which process it is.

2. Emit a stage boundary from the engine so the non-model stages are visible: a stage-start carrying the stage name and its role, and a stage-end carrying whether it passed. runStages (internal/drain/issue.go:322) is where every stage after implement is dispatched and is the natural place. Note the contract documented in internal/drain/bus.go: every event kind is handled by every renderer, so a new kind means the plain renderer, the JSON renderer and the TUI together.

Layout: colState is 8 cells (internal/tui/model.go:783). 'reviewer' fits exactly, 'integrator' does not, and a configured role name can be anything. Decide between widening the column, adding a STAGE column of its own, and truncating — and whichever it is, do not let it shift the ISSUE column, which the two-cell selection marker was deliberately built to keep stable.

The State vocabulary is documented at internal/tui/model.go:21-35 as the display's own, deliberately not drain.Outcome. Extending it with roles is consistent with that, but update the comment: it currently says a row spends most of its life in states an outcome has no name for, and this makes that more true, not less.
acceptance_criteria: A running row names the process that is running — worker, reviewer, integrator or a configured stage role — rather than 'running'. A gate or a 'run' stage is visible as itself, not as a stalled worker. Terminal rows are unchanged. 'killing' and 'asking' still override the cell. The ISSUE column does not move when a longer role name appears. The plain and JSON renderers handle any new event kind. Tests in internal/tui/model_test.go feed activity events with each role and assert the rendered cell; a screenshot scene covers a wave with a worker, a reviewer and a gate running at once.
notes: Ordered before beads-auto-imp-j5a.1 deliberately. Both rewrite the same parts of internal/tui/model.go — the Row struct, apply()'s EventActivity branch, line() and the key handler — and this epic exists partly because two issues editing one file in the same wave is how a drain parks work it had already finished. The detail view is also easier once the row already knows which role produced what.
close_reason: Closed

title: Refill a wave's freed slot instead of holding it idle until the barrier
description:
A wave is planned at exactly the concurrency cap and never grows. internal/wave/plan.go:75 stops filling at opt.Concurrency, and internal/drain/drain_wave.go:395 runs that fixed set behind a semaphore of the same size. The semaphore does release a slot when a worker ends — but the wave has no further issues to hand it, so the slot stays empty until every sibling finishes and the barrier has merged, gated and reviewed.

So with concurrency 3 and ten in-scope issues, one issue parking in its first minute means two workers for the rest of the wave while eight rows sit in the table saying 'waiting'. A parked issue is not doing anything; it should not be holding a slot.

What can actually be dispatched into a freed slot is whatever bd already calls ready and the scope allows, minus what the run has handled. That is the same question wave.Plan already answers — it is only ever asked once per wave.
design:
Ask again when a slot frees. In runWave (internal/drain/drain_wave.go:395), after a worker releases the semaphore, re-plan against bd, subtract what is in flight, done or parked, intersect with the scope, and dispatch into the free slot up to the concurrency cap.

Hazards, all of which have to be handled:

- The top-up joins the CURRENT wave. wave.Record (internal/wave/plan.go:141) increments s.Wave and resets WaveIssues, so it cannot be reused; a join path is needed that appends to WaveIssues, Attempts and InFlight under the same lock.
- bd ready stays the authority on what may start. An issue blocked on a sibling still in flight will not be offered, and that is correct — do not second-guess it.
- Do not top up after an outage. An OutcomeInfra report cancels the wave's context (drain_wave.go:448) precisely so five workers do not walk into the same wall; refilling would undo that. Same for a human Stop and for a cancelled parent context.
- Never exceed the cap. The semaphore stays the enforcement point.
- Emit an event, so the table shows the row joining wave N rather than a worker appearing from nowhere. bus.go documents the contract that every renderer handles every kind (AllEventKinds), so a new kind means updating the plain, JSON and TUI renderers together — reusing EventIssueStart with the right wave number may be the cheaper answer.
- Do not spin. bd offering nothing must not become a hot loop of 'bd ready' calls; only ask when a slot actually frees.
- The barrier still integrates the whole grown wave, which the All: true integrate already does.

Consider whether the same argument applies to the first wave: an issue parked by parkOutOfScope before dispatch never occupied a slot, so the initial plan can already be short. Check whether it should plan up to the cap after subtracting those.
acceptance_criteria: With a fake bd offering five in-scope ready issues and concurrency 2, an issue that parks immediately causes a third to be dispatched before the barrier. In-flight never exceeds the configured concurrency at any point. An infra failure still stops the wave, and nothing is topped up after it; the same for a stop from the TUI. Run state records the joined issues in the current wave, with correct attempt numbers, so an interrupted run resumes them. The TUI shows a topped-up issue as part of the wave it joined. A run where bd offers nothing new makes no extra bd calls beyond one per freed slot.
notes: Design decision the issue left open: a top-up is filtered by wave.Joinable before it joins. bd offers a dependent issue the moment its blocker closes, but the blocker's branch is not in HEAD until the barrier merges it, and a worker branches from the main checkout's HEAD — so joining would put a worker on a tree its dependency's work is missing from. Held back for the next wave instead. This is not second-guessing bd's readiness; it is the base-branch invariant the barrier exists for, and it is what keeps a wave a set of mutually independent issues (see wave.Order). Independent ready work — the case the issue describes — joins as specified.
close_reason: Closed

title: A sibling running in the same wave is never a blocker: say so in the worker prompt, and report it when a worker claims otherwise
description:
Reported from a live run in another repo: a worker declared its issue out of scope until another issue running in the same wave finished, and stopped.

By construction that claim is false about dependencies. A wave is bd's own ready front intersected with the run's scope (internal/wave/plan.go:67, which trusts 'bd ready' precisely because bd ready is blocker-aware), so no member of a wave holds a 'blocks' edge over another member. If a worker genuinely needs another issue's output, the graph is missing that edge — and the run cannot know it, because nobody wrote it down.

Two halves to this, and neither is worth doing alone.

The prompt half: prompts/worker.md:9-11 tells the worker that other workers are running right now on other issues, and then never returns to it. Step 7 (line 91) offers 'genuinely blocked' as an option with no guidance about what does and does not count. A model reading that, on an issue whose code touches the same area as a sibling's, reasonably concludes it should wait.

The reporting half: when a worker does park itself naming a sibling, the run should say so as what it is — a missing dependency edge — rather than leaving a human to read a park reason and guess. bd-auto knows the wave's members (runstate WaveIssues), so a park reason mentioning one of them is a cheap and specific signal.
design:
Prompt: add a short section to prompts/worker.md near 'Where you are'. A sibling running beside you is not a blocker. You are on your own branch cut from the base, its work merges after yours has been gated and reviewed separately, and waiting for it is waiting for something that cannot arrive during your turn. If your issue truly cannot be done without another issue's output, that is a missing dependency in the graph: do not park for it — record it as a discovery naming the issue and the edge that is missing, do whatever part of your issue does not depend on it, and say plainly in your final message what you could not do and why.

Reporting: when an issue is parked, compare the reason against the current wave's other members (runstate.State.WaveIssues). A hit is recorded as its own note on the run and carried in the report, phrased as a missing 'blocks' edge with the exact 'bd dep add <issue> <sibling>' a human would run. Do not add the edge automatically — a graph edited by an agent on the strength of a model's sentence is worse than a missing edge.

Depends on beads-auto-imp-j5a.3: until a self-park is recorded as a park at all, there is no park reason to inspect.
acceptance_criteria: prompts/worker.md tells a worker that concurrent siblings are not blockers and what to do instead; prompts/prompts_test.go covers the new text if it asserts on prompt content. A park whose reason names another issue in the same wave is reported distinctly, with the bd dep add command a human would run, and is visible in the drain report and the run's notes. No dependency edge is ever created automatically. A test parks an issue with a sibling's ID in the reason and asserts the report says so.
close_reason: Closed

title: Enter opens the selected issue's transcript in a Claude Code-style detail view
description:
The wave table is one line per issue and that line is all there is. Row.Detail holds the last thing that happened and the partial-message buffer is capped at 400 runes (internal/tui/model.go:95); everything before that is dropped. A human watching a worker that has been on the same tool call for four minutes has no way to ask what it is doing.

The keymap has no enter binding today — internal/tui/model.go:257 handles up/down, k and q only, and Selected() (model.go:512) already gives the row under the cursor.

The data exists in two places:

- Live: drain.EventActivity carries Role, Tool, Text and Phase (internal/drain/bus.go). But runner.Event (internal/runner/runner.go:343) carries a tool NAME and no tool input, so 'Bash(go test ./...)' cannot be rendered from the live stream as it stands.
- On disk: every model process writes its full stream-json transcript to .beads/auto/logs/<issue>-a<attempt>-r<round>-<role>.jsonl — drain.LogPath (internal/drain/drain.go:594), set at internal/drain/issue.go:472 and :481 for the worker and each stage, and internal/drain/integrate.go:514 for the integrator. That file has everything the view wants: assistant text, tool_use blocks with their input, tool_result blocks with is_error, and the result line with usage and cost. Nothing reads these files today.

The detail view should look like a Claude Code session, not like a log dump: assistant prose as wrapped text, each tool call as a header line carrying the tool name and a one-line argument summary, its result indented underneath and truncated with a marker for what was cut, errors in the failure colour, and a separator between rounds and stages naming the role that ran.
design:
Read the on-disk transcripts as the primary source. They cover what the live stream cannot — earlier rounds, earlier attempts, the reviewer and integrator stages, and a run that has already finished — and they carry tool inputs, which runner.Event does not. Use the live event stream only for the tail of the process currently running, or extend runner.Event with a short tool-input summary if the tail matters more than the extra field costs.

Reuse the adaptive lipgloss palette already in internal/tui/model.go:755-776 so the view is legible in light and dark terminals; do not introduce a second colour vocabulary.

Keys: enter opens the selected row, esc closes back to the table with the cursor where it was, up/down and pgup/pgdn scroll, g/G jump to either end. The question box takes keystrokes first (model.go:262) and enter already answers a question there, so the detail view must only open when Question() is nil — a human answering a prompt must not have the screen replaced underneath them.

Bound the memory. Five workers streaming partial messages for an hour is a lot of text; page the file rather than holding all of it, or keep a fixed-size window.
acceptance_criteria: Pressing enter on a selected row opens that issue's transcript; esc returns to the table with the cursor unmoved. The view scrolls and clamps at both ends. Tool calls render with their name and an argument summary, results indented and truncated. A row whose worker has not started yet says so rather than showing an empty pane. The table keeps folding events in underneath, so closing and re-opening shows what arrived meanwhile. Enter still answers a question when the ask box is up. Tests in internal/tui/model_test.go press the keys and assert on View(); new scenes are added to internal/tui/screenshot_test.go and scripts/tui-shots.sh, with screenshots committed under docs/screenshots/tui.

title: An unparked retry overwrites the transcript of the attempt it is retrying
description:
Drain 2 killed kv-555.4 mid-flight, parked it, and was then told to unpark and retry. `run unpark` resets the attempt counter — deliberately, it is a retry budget — so the retry's worker ran as attempt 1 again, and LogPath named the same file the killed attempt had written. The runner opens it with os.Create, which truncates. The killed attempt's transcript is gone: .beads/auto/logs/ has one kv-555.4-a1-r0-worker.jsonl and it is the retry's.

That transcript is the only record of what the killed worker did before it died, which is exactly what somebody investigating a kill wants to read. It is also the thing the run's own usage accounting is reconciled against, so a clobbered log makes the per-process table silently disagree with the run total.

The identity issue+attempt+round+role stops being unique the moment attempts are reset, so the path has to cope: keep the existing name when it is free and take the next free -N suffix when it is not.
acceptance_criteria: A second process with the same issue, attempt, round and role writes beside the first rather than over it; a test asserts the earlier transcript still reads back after the retry.
close_reason: the claude adapter creates transcripts with O_EXCL and takes the next free -N when the name is taken, reporting back where it actually wrote; TestASecondProcessWritesBesideTheFirstTranscriptRatherThanOverIt

title: record turns alongside cost and tokens
description: The claude CLI reports num_turns on its result line, bd-auto already parses that line for cost and tokens, and then drops the turn count on the floor. It is the one number that says how much work a process actually did rather than how much it cost, and it is what separates a worker that solved something in four turns from one that ground through forty for the same money. Today the only way to get it is to read .beads/auto/logs/*.jsonl by hand.
acceptance_criteria: runner.Usage carries turns and sums them; the claude adapter fills it from the result line; the run report and the pull request body say how many turns the run took; a stream test covers it.

title: the wave table's last line is erased on exit, so the finished view is never seen
description:
Two faults that meet at the same line.

bubbletea's standard renderer writes the final frame on a graceful shutdown and then, in stop(), erases the line the cursor is on — which is the last line of that frame. Verified against v1.3.10 with a three-line probe program: the third line is gone from the pane after the program exits. For this view the last line is keys(), so every drain that ends normally loses its key line off the bottom of the final frame.

And the finished branch of keys() promises 'the run is over · q to close', which is not a thing that can happen: finishedMsg sets finished and returns tea.Quit in the same Update, so no keystroke is ever handled while finished is true. The one line the user is told to press a key at is the line they never see, and the key would do nothing if they did.

Found by photographing the run-end scene in scripts/tui-shots.sh: the finished capture is the run-end capture minus its last line.
acceptance_criteria: The final frame keeps every line it rendered, including the key line; the finished key line says what is true rather than offering a keystroke that cannot be pressed; a test covers both, and the finished screenshot shows the complete frame.

title: config show omits the ask block, so the one setting with a surprising default cannot be read back
description: The config file's own header says `bd-auto config show` prints the resolved values, and it prints every block except ask. That is the block a reader most needs resolved: enabled defaults to on, roles deliberately excludes the reviewer, and hold and timeout are the two numbers that decide whether a question survives a backend's idle limit. Found while setting up the kv test lab: the lab config sets all four and config show reported none of them, so there was no way to confirm the file had been read.
acceptance_criteria: config show emits an ask object with enabled, timeout, hold and roles; timeout 0 means wait forever and is reported as 0 rather than as a negative duration; a test covers the defaults and an override.

title: Put a bar on what a worker files as discovered work
description:
Worker prompt step 6 currently says 'file anything you discovered' with no threshold, and the backlog shows what that buys: 1.54 new issues per issue worked, and issues like beads-auto-imp-r4a which is a limitation the worker verified and then wrote into a code comment — filed as work that can never be completed by implementing anything.

The bar belongs in bd-auto's own worker prompt, not in beads' init template, because bd-auto is what spawns the worker and prompts/worker.md is the half of the contract bd-auto owns.

State the test as something a worker can apply: would a human schedule this as a separate piece of work? A limitation you documented where it lives is documented. A restatement of the issue you just finished is not a discovery.

title: Cut a refused round short instead of paying for the whole flail
description:
Found while fixing beads-auto-imp-o4q. The CLI reports permission_denials only on its final result line, so the engine cannot act until the process has already finished. In the case that motivated o4q that was 226 seconds and 0.41 USD of a worker trying git update-index, the update-config skill and touch, all refused, before anything could notice.

o4q stops the run after that one round instead of burning the whole attempt, which is most of the win. What is still paid for is the round itself.

The denial is visible mid-stream, in the tool_result whose text is 'Claude requested permissions to write to <path>, but you havent granted it yet'. The adapter could watch for it and cancel the process on, say, the third refusal in a row with no successful tool call in between, and report the same reason. Weigh it carefully: this is string matching against a CLI message rather than the structured array, so it will rot, and killing a run on a heuristic is how a legitimately-recovering worker gets cut off. Measure how often the pattern actually appears before building on it.

title: Report the tools a scoped reviewer was refused
description:
Result.Denials now carries the tools a backend refused (added by beads-auto-imp-o4q for the worker's no-progress path). Nothing reads it for a judging stage.

A reviewer runs under permissions: scoped with a fixed allowlist, so it is refused things by design and that is correct. What is missing is any report of it: if the allowlist is too narrow for a repo, the reviewer quietly returns a weaker verdict on less evidence and nobody finds out. agentStage could log the refused tool names alongside the verdict, or write them into the review notes at .beads/auto/review/<id>.md, so a repo can widen allowed_tools on evidence rather than on a guess.

Not a failure path: a scoped denial must stay non-fatal. This is reporting only.

title: beads' jsonl re-import reverts bd-auto's live bd writes, not just the failure notes
description:
Wider case left uncovered by beads-auto-imp-so5, which only made the RETRY FEEDBACK independent of bd by carrying it in run state.

The mechanism is not specific to notes. beads sets core.hooksPath=.beads/hooks; post-checkout and post-merge both run 'bd hooks run <hook>', which imports .beads/issues.jsonl over the Dolt database. Any checkout-shaped git operation therefore reverts every bd write made since the jsonl on the incoming ref was exported.

Observed live in this repo during the so5 session: a 'git pull --rebase' in the main checkout silently reverted 8 issues from closed back to open.

Confirmed in this repo, non-destructively, while fixing so5:
  - core.hooksPath is .beads/hooks and post-checkout is installed
  - a clone of this repo showed the hook invoking 'bd import' on 'git worktree add'
  - 'bd import --dry-run' of HEAD:.beads/issues.jsonl over the live DB reported 'Would import 50 issues', with so5 recorded as open in the jsonl while the DB had it in_progress

What is still exposed during a bd-auto run:
  - a worker closing its issue, then any wave barrier merge / worktree creation reverting it to open
  - BD.Park's reason and status on a parked issue
  - BD.Reset between attempts
  - the integrator's epic close
Run state keeps its own copy of done/parked/attempts, so bd-auto's control flow survives; what does not survive is the state a HUMAN reads out of bd afterwards, and any decision bd-auto re-derives from bd rather than from run state.

The hooks belong to beads, not to bd-auto, so the fix is unlikely to be 'change the hooks'. Candidates worth weighing:
  - re-assert bd-auto's own view of an issue after any operation that can fire the hook (a reconcile pass at each barrier, driven from run state)
  - set BEADS_HOOK_TIMEOUT or an env guard around bd-auto's own git operations, if beads offers one

title: permissions: auto refuses a headless worker every file write
description:
Found while building the resume-vs-fresh measurement (wz9.7).

With runners.default.permissions: auto — the shipped default — a 'claude -p' worker in a throwaway git repo was refused every Write and every shell redirect: 'Claude requested permissions to write to <path inside its own worktree>, but you haven't granted it yet.' Headless there is nobody to grant it, so the worker looped for 226 seconds and $0.41 trying alternatives (git update-index, the update-config skill, touch), changed nothing, and the attempt died on the no-progress check.

The experiment switched to permissions: bypass and the same worker wrote files immediately.

Unclear whether this reproduces in this repo's own worktrees — the temp repo may simply not have been a trusted project — but the default is 'auto', the failure mode is a whole attempt of silent flailing at full price, and no-progress reads as 'the model did nothing' rather than 'the model was not allowed to'. Worth reproducing under .beads/auto/wt/ here before a real drain relies on it.

If it does reproduce, two things are wanted: a permission denial should classify as something other than work-failed, and the default should be one that can actually write.
notes:
REPRODUCED here, not only in the throwaway repo. claude 2.1.233, in a directory under this repo own .beads/auto/wt/, argv matching the adapter for permissions: auto.
  --permission-mode auto              Write REFUSED ("Claude requested permissions to write to <path>, but you havent granted it yet").
  --permission-mode acceptEdits       Write allowed, plain Bash ("go version", "git init") REFUSED.
  --permission-mode bypassPermissions both allowed, file written immediately.
The refused run exits 0 and reports subtype "success", is_error false. So classify() returned ClassOK: the engine was not even reaching work-failed, it reached the no-progress check, which fails the attempt outright and reads as "the model did nothing". The refusal is visible in exactly one place, the result lines structured permission_denials array, and that is what the fix reads rather than string-matching tool_result text.

DECISION 1, classification. A denial is not a class by itself: a run can be refused one tool, route around it and finish, and the reviewer is scoped on purpose so it is refused things by design. The signal is the pair, refused a tool AND changed nothing. That is now OutcomeInfra instead of OutcomeFailed: costs neither a round nor an attempt, parks nothing, stops the run with the permission level to change. Deliberately NOT ClassInfraFailed at the runner seam, because that class is Recoverable() and would spend all 5 infra retries plus ~75s of backoff re-running a request refused identically every time. This path retries zero times, which is the right number for a refusal.

DECISION 2, shipped default auto -> bypass (internal/config/runners.go builtinRunners; the templates runners block is commented out so it only documents it). Security-relevant, so stated plainly: headless there is nobody to grant a permission, so "ask a human" is not a safer default, it is a default that cannot do the job. auto burns a whole attempt at full price and misreports the cause; acceptEdits still cannot run the gate, git or bd. What actually contains a worker is structural and independent of the permission mode: a throwaway worktree under .beads/auto/, its own branch, gitguard hooks refusing push/merge/rebase, Verify failing closed, and a scope a human confirmed before anything spawned. The reviewer stays scoped, because none of that argument applies to a role that only reads and a reviewer that can run bare Bash is a reviewer that can push.

Also added, per explicit request on top of the issue: --dangerously-skip-permissions on both `bd-auto drain` and `bd-auto issue run`, same spelling as Claude Codes own flag, shared help text so the two cannot drift. It forces bypass on every role including the reviewer, and warns on stderr that it did.
USER DECISION, supersedes DECISION 2 above. The shipped default stays `auto`. The bypass-default reasoning recorded above was put to the user directly, with the containment argument stated fairly, and they chose flag-only: a flag is opt-in, and shipping bypass as the default was not authorised. Treat DECISION 2 as the REJECTED ALTERNATIVE, already considered and declined by the user. Do not reopen it.

Reverted: internal/config/runners.go builtinRunners back to PermAuto, plus the prose in template.go, .beads-auto.yaml and README.md, and the config test assertions. TestTheDefaultWorkerCanWrite was rewritten as TestBypassIsNeverTheShippedDefault, which pins the decision and names the rejected argument in its comment so a future reader does not have to rediscover it.

Everything else stands as built, including --dangerously-skip-permissions applying to ALL roles, the reviewer included. The user was asked specifically about excluding the reviewer and chose to keep it uniform.

CONSEQUENCE, stated plainly. With the default at auto, a plain `bd-auto drain` with no flag WILL still hit the measured failure: workers refused every write, one round burned at full price. Nothing in this change prevents that; what it changes is that the failure is now legible instead of silent. The auto path surfaces it as OutcomeInfra with deniedReason naming the refused tools and pointing at permissions: bypass and --dangerously-skip-permissions, it costs neither a round nor an attempt, and it parks nothing. Anyone who wants a drain that completes must opt in, per repo or per run. README has a Permissions section saying so in bold.

Two review nits also fixed. deniedReason now takes the permission level and gives advice that fits it: under bypass it points at a PreToolUse hook, a deny rule or a managed policy rather than at .beads-auto.yaml, which cannot be the cause of a refusal on bypass. The drain.go comment about the preview was accurate — preview() does print each role permission level in its Models block — so it was reworded to say where, and TestThePreviewNamesEachRolesPermissionLevel now pins it, including that the flag changes what the table shows.

title: beads' post-checkout hook wipes bd-auto's failure notes, so a fresh retry starts blind
description:
Found while building the resume-vs-fresh measurement (wz9.7). Reproduced deterministically with git alone, no models involved.

A fresh attempt gets no feedback in its prompt: drain.attempt() starts each attempt with an empty feedback string, so workerPrompt renders the plain task and tells the worker to read the issue's notes. The failure notes ARE therefore the whole feedback channel for the retry path.

They do not survive. beads installs core.hooksPath=.beads/hooks, whose pre-commit EXPORTS the database to .beads/issues.jsonl and whose post-checkout IMPORTS that file back over the database. The sequence bd-auto runs is:

  1. worker commits in its worktree     -> pre-commit exports the DB to issues.jsonl on the branch
  2. the attempt fails
  3. noteFailure writes the reason to the issue  (DB only; nothing is committed)
  4. discardAttempt removes the worktree and deletes the branch, taking the exported jsonl with it
  5. worktree.Ensure creates the next attempt's worktree from base
     -> post-checkout imports the BASE jsonl over the DB, reverting everything since step 1

Step 5 deletes the note written in step 3. Verified in a throwaway repo: a note written before the worker's commit survives; a note written after it (which is where bd-auto writes) is gone the moment the next attempt's worktree is created.

Observed live first: a fresh-heavy run (max_rounds 1, retry 3) over a fixture issue burned all four attempts. The attempt-2 transcript shows the worker ran 'bd show' and got no NOTES section at all, so it repeated attempt 1's mistake exactly, three times, at full price.

Asymmetric by construction: resume rounds keep the feedback in the prompt and never re-create the worktree, so they are unaffected. Only the fresh-retry path is broken, and it fails silently — the engine's warning is discarded whenever Log is nil, which is what --quiet does.

Worth checking whether the same holds in this repo (it has the same hooks) before trusting retry to recover anything.

title: Worker commits pick up .beads/issues.jsonl churn from other workers
description:
gitguard chains beads' own pre-commit hook into every worker worktree, which is correct: it keeps .beads/issues.jsonl in sync. But issues.jsonl is a tracked file exporting the SHARED dolt database, so a worker committing in its worktree stages an export reflecting every other worker's bd writes as well as its own. buys), accumulated cost per issue and for the run, and wave/attempt state.

Plus the control channel, which ships in the same issue because it is the only
way to abandon a run in flight: k kills the selected worker, q / ctrl-c stops
the run with state intact. Both depend on the process-group kill from the claude
adapter; killing the direct child only would leave a go test running and its
worktree held.

Cost is displayed, never enforced. Nothing here is a budget. With scope chosen
up front the run is already bounded; this is so you can watch it and change your
mind.

Non-TTY falls back to the plain renderer from the drain issue.

- Live wave table with per-worker activity, per-issue and run-total cost.
- k kills the selected worker: the process AND its children die, and the issue is

- q stops the run with state intact; re-running drain resumes the interrupted

- Non-TTY falls back to the plain renderer with no TUI code on the path.

title: prompts/: rewrite the three role prompts for headless execution
description:
agents/*.md are subagent definitions, not role prompts, and converting them is a
rewrite rather than a frontmatter strip.

bd-worker.md alone carries: the BD-AUTO: footer protocol (hook.go:215, being
deleted), "your report is the only thing that reaches the orchestrator" and its
25-line cap (there is no orchestrator context left to protect), "a hook blocks
those anyway" (there is no hook), and a Shell section about Claude Code refusing
statically unverifiable commands under worktree isolation, which does not apply
to a plain claude -p in a plain worktree.

Every role prompt also gains an explicit override of the repo's own CLAUDE.md,
which says "Work is NOT complete until git push succeeds... NEVER stop before
pushing." A headless claude -p loads CLAUDE.md exactly like an interactive
session. Today the PreToolUse deny answers that with an actionable message;
afterwards the worker gets a bare git hook rejection and, told push is
mandatory, retries or reaches for git pull --rebase, which is the rebase hole
gitguard has to close. The prompt says in as many words: you are one attempt
inside a bd-auto run, you commit to your own branch and stop, the integrator
merges, nothing here pushes.

Early on purpose: issues from the pipeline onward cannot spawn anything without
these.

description:
The eqc.13 dogfood run drained a real epic with the plugin loaded, but wave 1 was a single issue, so the parallel path was never watched live. Deterministic coverage exists in make smoke; agent behaviour under contention does not.

Set up a throwaway epic of 3-4 genuinely independent issues, at least two of which touch the same file so the integrator meets a real conflict. Run with --autonomy wave so there is a barrier to inspect.

title: Dogfood run: drain a real epic with the plugin loaded
description:
Point the finished tool at a real epic in this repo and let it drain, with the author watching. Record what actually happened: orchestrator context growth per issue, wall-clock versus a sequential baseline, how many issues needed a retry, how many merges conflicted.

Write the README from that run rather than from the design: install, config reference for .beads-auto.yaml, how to add a custom pipeline stage, how to stop a run, and how to recover a parked issue.

This epic is itself the natural first target once enough of the pipeline exists.
acceptance_criteria: One epic drained end to end without manual intervention beyond approvals, with measurements recorded on this issue and a README a stranger could follow.
notes:
README is written and committed (install, config reference, custom stage guide, required repo settings, failure handling, design notes).

What remains is the live run, which cannot be done from inside an ordinary session because it needs the plugin loaded:

  make build
  claude --plugin-dir /home/dude-lt/dev/beads-auto-imp
  /bd-auto <epic-id>

Everything below is deterministic and already covered by `make check` (unit) and `make smoke` (end to end against a throwaway epic): run state, wave planning, DAG exclusion, all five hooks, retry-then-park, merge ordering, rehydration.

What only a live run can verify, because it is agent behaviour rather than code:
- a bd-worker actually staying inside its worktree and its report budget
- bd-reviewer verdict quality and the send-back-to-same-worker loop
- bd-integrator resolving a genuine merge conflict between two workers
- whether the Stop hook keeps the orchestrator on task across a real autocompact

Measure during the run: orchestrator context growth per issue, wall clock vs a sequential baseline, retries needed, merges that conflicted. Record the numbers here and fold anything surprising back into the README.

Suggested first target: a small epic of 3-4 genuinely independent issues. Start with --autonomy wave so there is a barrier to inspect before it drains further.
DOGFOOD RUN, 2026-08-14 14:23 UTC. Epic beads-auto-imp-eqc drained with the plugin loaded (concurrency 5, autonomy auto). 12 of 13 children were already closed, so wave 1 was a single issue: this one. The worker implementing it ran under the orchestrator it was documenting.

MEASURED
- orchestrator overhead, run start to wave 1 dispatched: 8s (14:23:19 -> 14:23:27)
- retries: 0 | parked: 0 | merge conflicts: 0 (one branch in the wave)
- manual intervention: none beyond permission approvals
- orchestrator context growth per issue: not observable from inside the worker. The per-issue cost the design controls is the capped worker report; measuring real growth needs the multi-worker run filed as discovered work.

VERIFIED LIVE, not by test double
- PreToolUse binding recorded agent a42782c5c6276e01e -> eqc.13 from the worker's own claim call, with nothing passed in naming the issue.
- The integration guard denied a real integration command typed by a real worker.
- bd resolved the main repo DB from inside the worktree with no setup; show/create/close/delete all worked.
- The gate ran green inside the worktree.

NOT PROVEN BY A ONE-ISSUE WAVE
parallel workers under contention, the integrator resolving a genuine conflict, the reviewer send-back loop, retry-then-park, and the Stop hook across a real autocompact. All are covered deterministically by make smoke; none has been watched with several real agents in flight.

DEFECTS FOUND BY DOGFOODING, all fixed on this branch
1. No way to retry a parked issue. Parking excludes via run state, not just bd status, so reopening in bd alone did nothing and recovery meant hand-editing run.json. Added: bd-auto run unpark --issue <id>.
2. scripts/smoke.sh would have destroyed this live run. Its cleanup stops the run and deletes .beads/auto, and run state is shared with the main checkout even from a worktree. It now refuses while a run is active, and both preflight checks moved above the EXIT trap so bailing out no longer runs cleanup.
3. The integration guard matched its pattern anywhere in the command string, so writing this very note was denied for quoting an integration command. Now anchored to command position. This is what blocked the first attempt to record these measurements.
4. Worktree isolation is stricter than documented: a worker cannot cd to the main checkout for any git command, and a plain five-command chain is refused as unverifiable.
5. bd-auto on a worker's PATH is the main checkout's binary, i.e. the running orchestrator's build. A worker changing bd-auto must invoke ./bin/bd-auto or it silently tests the old binary.

README updated with all of the above, plus how to stop a run and how to recover a parked issue.
CORRECTION after review. Defect 3 above says the integration guard was fixed by anchoring the match to command position. That fix was wrong and is superseded: anchoring closed the false positive but opened real bypasses (a sudo prefix, an env assignment prefix, nohup, a loop body, an if condition), any of which would have let a worker integrate. The guard now keeps the original anywhere-match and blanks out single- and double-quoted spans before applying it, so quoted text is treated as data without narrowing what counts as a command. All five bypasses are in the blocked table and were checked against the built binary, not only in unit tests.

Also from review: the new unpark steps in scripts/smoke.sh had made the parked-rendering assertion vacuous, because they returned the issue to the run before the rehydration check and the bare ID then matched the in-flight line. The unpark steps moved below that check, which now asserts the literal parked-line prefix and also verifies the line disappears once the issue is unparked.
SECOND CORRECTION, final review round. Blanking quoted spans was itself unsound in two ways, both caught in review and both letting a worker integrate: executor forms (eval, xargs, and the -c form of sh and its variants) run their quoted payload, so blanking it hid the payload; and an unbalanced quote blanked everything to end of input, where an apostrophe in a trailing # comment was enough to hide the next line that the shell still runs. The guard now falls back to matching the raw command in both cases, and the strip helper reports whether it ended inside a quote instead of silently returning a truncated string. The original quoted-note case still passes.

Worth recording as a dogfood lesson: three review rounds on this one guard, each fix opening the opposite hole. Round 1 over-fired on quoted data; round 2 anchored to command position and let sudo, env, nohup, loops and if-conditions through; round 3 stripped quotes and let executors and unbalanced quotes through. A guard whose input is an arbitrary shell string has no clean regex answer, only a deliberate bias. The bias chosen here is to fall back to the broadest match whenever the parse is uncertain, since a false positive costs one rephrasing and a false negative costs an unreviewed merge.

title: PreToolUse hook: agent-to-issue binding and merge guard
description:
PreToolUse hooks fire inside subagents and carry agent_id and agent_type. Match on Bash and inspect the command.

Binding: when a worker runs bd update <id> --claim or bd ready --claim, record agent_id -> issue in the run state. That mapping is what lets SubagentStop verify the right issue and what would later enable per-worker file-ownership rules.

Merge guard: deny a worker any git merge, rebase onto main, or push. Only the integrator merges, and only at the wave barrier. Denying this deterministically is far more reliable than asking the worker not to.
acceptance_criteria: After a worker claims, run state contains its agent_id -> issue binding. A worker attempting git merge main is denied with an explanatory reason; the integrator is not.
close_reason: PreToolUse claim binding + merge guard; regexes unit-tested, both paths smoke-tested

title: SubagentStop verification hook
description:
When a worker finishes, independently verify it actually reached a terminal state rather than trusting its report: the issue is closed, or blocked with notes, and a bd-auto/<id> branch exists with a commit. If not, exit 2 to keep the worker running with a precise reason.

This closes the gap where an agent announces success without having done the bookkeeping. Depends on knowing which issue the finishing agent owned, which is what the PreToolUse claim-binding issue provides; fall back to parsing the required report footer when no binding exists.
acceptance_criteria: A worker that reports done without closing its issue is sent back with a specific reason instead of being accepted.
close_reason: SubagentStop verification incl. footer fallback and fail-open; smoke-tested all four paths

title: A continuous run gates the same tree twice at the end of every run
description:
internal/drain/drain_cont.go ends with a settling barrier — Integrate{All: true} — because reconcile, the discovered-work filing and the epic decision each have to happen exactly once at the end of a run, and a continuous run has no other barrier to hang them on. That barrier also runs the full gate (the `if rep.Stopped == ""` block in Integrate), on a tree that has not moved since the last lane integration gated it green: every issue was merged and gated as it landed, and every worker has finished by then, so nothing can have changed in between.

On a repo whose gate is a full test suite that is minutes added to every run, for an answer already known. A fix would let Integrate skip gateRepo when it merged nothing and HEAD is where the last green gate left it — rep.Head == rep.BaseHead is already computed for the index refresh, and the run's own last IntegrateReport already says whether that tree passed. The gate must still run whenever anything merged, because 'green on the fully merged epic branch' is what the handoff rests on.

Found by the bd-auto worker on beads-auto-imp-04l.2, and filed at the wave barrier — deferred, so it waits for a human rather than being offered to the next run.

title: tui-shots.sh leaves captures behind when a scene is renamed or renumbered
description:
scripts/tui-shots.sh writes each capture as <prefix>-NN-<name>.ansi/.png into docs/screenshots/tui and never removes anything. The scene numbers come from the scene's position in internal/tui/screenshot_test.go, so inserting one renumbers every scene after it and the whole tail is written under new names while the old files stay.

That had already happened once: the barrier scenes (tui-12-barrier-gating, tui-13-barrier-red-gate) pushed everything after them along, and 19 stale pairs — tui-12-wave-integrated through tui-30-finished — sat in the directory photographing a display that had moved on. This issue deleted that batch by hand, and nothing stops the next insertion leaving the same mess.

The script knows exactly what it wrote: it prints every stem as it captures it. Collecting those and removing anything else in $OUT at the end would make the directory always be the current scene list and nothing else.

Found by the bd-auto worker on beads-auto-imp-04l.6, and filed at the wave barrier — deferred, so it waits for a human rather than being offered to the next run.

title: The wave table is 67 cells wide whatever the terminal is, so it wraps below that
description:
internal/tui/model.go:header() formats the column headings with no clip() at all, and the fixed columns it lays out add up to 67 cells (2 marker + 22 issue + 4 wave + 11 state + 6 time + 8 cost + separators + 8 of ACTIVITY). line() then floors the activity column at 8 cells — room := maxInt(m.width()-lipgloss.Width(fixed), 8) — so a row cannot come out narrower than 67 either.

On any terminal under 67 columns every heading and every row soft-wraps onto two lines, which doubles the table's height, breaks the alignment the eye tracks down, and makes windowTable's row arithmetic wrong (it counts rendered lines as one row each). The screenshot harness photographs a 'narrow' scene at 64 columns, three cells inside the fault.

A fix has to decide which column gives way below 67: clipping header() to m.width() is one line and stops the heading wrapping, but the rows need either a narrower ISSUE column, a dropped COST or WAVE column, or an accepted clip of the whole row at m.width(). Whichever it is, windowTable should count the lines it actually emits.

Found by the bd-auto worker on beads-auto-imp-04l.1, and filed at the wave barrier — deferred, so it waits for a human rather than being offered to the next run.

title: bd-auto worker status reports any run.json on disk as active
description:
internal/cmds/worker.go:216 returns a hard-coded "active": true for every state that loads, special-casing only runstate.ErrNoRun — the same misreport beads-auto-imp-gvg fixed in `bd-auto run status`. Against a standalone or stopped run it prints {"active": true, "in_flight": null, "wave": 0}, verified against a state file with status "standalone" and no in-flight entries. runstate.State.Active() now exists and answers this exactly; the fix is to report st.Active() there as run status does, so the two commands cannot disagree about whether a run is armed.

title: the README's wave table shows a cost for a running worker, which the shipped backend cannot report
description:
README's 'Watching a run' example gives running rows a cost — t-2 running at $0.4210 — and says the table shows 'what it has cost so far'. The claude CLI reports cost only on its result line, so a row's cost is a dash for the whole of its first model process and only appears once that process ends. Watched live on the kv-ctf drain: kv-ctf.1 showed '-' for its entire 1m45s implement stage and $0.7884 the instant it finished.

Nothing is wrong with the display — it is the honest rendering of a backend that has reported nothing yet, and the number does then accumulate across an issue's later stages, so a row in review shows what its implement stage cost. What is wrong is the example, which promises a live figure and is the first thing anyone reads about the table.
acceptance_criteria: The example table shows what a real run shows, and one sentence says when a cost appears.

title: Configure the beads Dolt remote for cross-machine issue sync
